narrative: During hot work activity, there was fire incident which impacted two contractor personnel. The more severely injured person was transferred to a specialist burn centre, but he unfortunately passed away.
what_went_wrong: Contractor personnel were performing planned hot work inside a tank on three stilling wells. These works were required to prepare the tank for calibration (hydrotesting) prior to returning the tank to service. IP1 was grinding datum plate bolts off stilling well 2. IP2 was welding a datum plate on the base of stilling well 3, approximately 1.7m away from stilling well 2. After removing two of the four bolts from stilling well 2, crude oil that had accumulated in its 2" compartment began flowing from stilling well 2, spraying in the direction of stilling well 3. Because of the welding or grinding work, the released crude oil ignited. Both IP1 and IP2 sustained burns in the resulting fire.
corrective_actions:
1. Tank certification as hydrocarbon free - tanks shall be certified as 'gas free' after tank draining and cleaning, in fact, free of residual hydrocarbons. Personnel certifying tanks shall be aware of all potential locations of residual hydrocarbons, including those where use of standard gas detector would be unlikely to detect their presence.
• Tank cleaning - Cleaned tanks shall be free of residual hydrocarbons. Tank cleaning personnel shall have 'front of mind' awareness of potential locations of residual hydrocarbons.
• Emergency notification - Emergency service personnel shall promptly and successfully notify in case of emergencies. A consistent (across assets/locations) and simple process shall be in place for company staff and contractor personnel to provide emergency notification.
• Personal protective equipment (PPE) - Contractor personnel shall understand and fully comply with the PPE Manual.
• DEP standard drawing for a stilling well - Company and contractor personnel should be skilled enough to understand and correctly interpret the drawing content.

narrative: A floorman was working at a BOP maintenance area at jack up cellar deck at a height of almost 17 meters from the platform top deck. After assembling the BOP shear rams, some housekeeping activities (including tools recovery and collection) were being performed by a crew of total six members. At the time of the incident, the IP was standing on the walking area of the BOP nearby the Coflex (right side of BOP). He had previously received some tools from height in order to recover them (at least a metal plate and a chain block, with total weight of approximately 15 kg) from one crew member standing on the left side of BOP, third floor. The IP approached the right side of the area, through the walking area around the BOP - passing in the rear side of BOP itself. Most likely his intention was to approach the BOP first floor from the right side to collect other tools or to place the received ones in a dedicated area, before the final collection. In any case he put his foot above the Coflex hose connected with the BOP (inherently slippery) and fell down through an open area of almost 1 metre (between the tubular handrail and the walking area around the BOP) from a height of 17 metres. The falling dynamic is compatible with both hypothesis: either the IP lost his balance due to the weight of the tools (approximately 15 kg) or while approaching the BOP first floor. A medevac was immediately activated but the IP was declared dead in the hospital.
what_went_wrong:
• Poor planning activities and role assignment: the IP started working on the POB area as part of BOP maintenance crew but then was sent to the shale shaker area. After finishing the activity there, the IP went back to the BOP area to recover his original task.
• Complacency and training/competences gaps: the IP and crew members demonstrated poor risk perception and awareness on working at height.
• Poor Risk Assessment: Job Safety Analysis was attached to the PTW but risks related to fall from height, manual handling, presence of slippery areas and absence of barriers were not included in the risk analysis.
• Incomplete operating instruction: Job Safety Analysis reported the list of main tasks for BOP maintenance(including method of statement) but this list did not include all the risks related to working at height. JSA did not include tasks and risks related to the lifting operations that were part of the activity and a dedicated permit to work for such activities was not issued.
• Tool Box Talk (TBT) not effective: TBT performed but crew did not flag the falling or slipping/tripping hazards and risks related to improper manual handling.
• PPE not used: the IP and some of the crew members not wearing the personnel fall protection equipment foreseen by the PTW.
• Work environment: presence of an open side in the BOP area of around 93 cm height between the first handrail and the floor. Such free space is wide enough to allow a person to fall through it. No other barriers and signs were present.
• Design specifications not respected: the top and mid rails of the handrail were installed at a height higher than as it shall be as per standards.
• MOC: installation of tubular handrails at height different than as per standard, not analyzed or risk assessed trough MOC process.
• Lack of supervision: supervision not effective and previous inspections did not identify the unsafe conditions of the working area.
• Poor Housekeeping: the hose that the IP stepped on was wet with oil and grease and thus slippery. The hose was beside the walkway area without segregation or barrier.
• Contractor Management: opportunities for improvement have been found in the contract management process, as new higher HSE requirements were included in the contract but only inspection for rig acceptance was done when hiring the Rig.
• Emergency Management & Response: delays in helicopter take-off due to some equipment to be loaded, medevac procedure not properly followed.
corrective_actions:
• All the risks related to Work at Height shall be evaluated (including tools handling), assessed in the Permit to Work and deeply discussed during the pre-job meetings, briefing and Tool Box Talk.
• Ensure all personnel involved in the operation are aware of the operating instructions and methods of statement.
• Refresh PTW procedure (including Tool Box Talk and Job Safety Analysis philosophy) and risks related to routine and non-routine activities. Ensure all personnel involved are aware of all the activity-related risks, duties & responsibilities, and safety precautions.
• Ensure opening of a dedicated PTW / Risk Assessment / Lifting Plan for any Lifting Operation requiring it.
• Ensure adequate supervision of activities.
• The worksite area shall be tidy before beginning a task, at the end of shifts and on completion of the task.
• All the Rig operators need to be aware of all the risks related to the activities.
• In cooperation with a third party, assess the competences, duties, rig organization to understand if sufficient, skilled manpower is available at the rig to perform the activities, as per duties and planning. Ensure periodic follow up of 3rd party inspections/assessments.
• Ensure proper Contractor Management by implementing specific safety programs and initiatives and verifying contractor compliance with contract requirements (eventually with support of a third party verification).
• Provide barriers to prevent fall risk areas as much as possible, and safety signs to make the crews aware of the risk of falling and the presence of slippery areas and area segregations / no go zone.
• Clearly assign roles & responsibilities in the medevac procedure; periodically refresh all Rig Personnel about the Communication Flow Chart in case of medevac; perform regular medevac Drills without previous announcement/notification.

narrative: During Preventive Maintenance (PM) of emergency shutdown valve at a wellsite, the actuator of the valve abruptly burst and its metallic part hit a nearby contractor. The injured Person (IP) was taken to the clinic, where he passed away. The actuator detached parts hit the flow line Pressure Differential Transmitter (PDT) tubings, which resulted in minor crack on a Down Stream (D/S) welded nipple. This led to gas leakage.
what_went_wrong:
• Risk Assessment not revised following the deviation from Scope of Work (SOW).
• Tight schedule, only one Instrument team was on site to perform all the planned activities.
• Complacency due to routine activity being perceived as low risk, leading to overconfidence of workers.
• The Instrument Technicians themselves deviated from SOW without applying Management of Change process.
• Stop Work Authority not applied.
• Ineffective supervision. Supervisors were present on site, but focused on other activities.
• Lack of means of communication. Unavailability of radio device for communication between control room and work area leading to pressurized actuator for more than 7 minutes.
• Lack of awareness of performing authority related to process hazards leading to risk underestimation.
corrective_actions:
• Any change or deviation to design, asset, process, work procedure or practices shall be accurately identified, reported and assessed by competent and trained personnel.
• The job shall be suspended in case of change in the SOW, and Risk assessment revised to involve all the stakeholders.
• Ensure all personnel involved in the operation are aware of the operating instructions and methods of statement.
• Ensure proper communication among working team members on site.
• Ensure competence, awareness and training of the personnel involved in operations.

narrative: A Contractor's water tanker rolled over while it was travelling towards a right of way from a water point. There were two passengers in the tanker; a driver and a local person. Both were seriously injured during the accident. Medical treatment was provided to the local person at the hospital. The local person had been engaged by the deceased driver on the day of accident. The driver passed away while he was being transferred to hospital by ambulance.
what_went_wrong: The driver did not go to a lower gear on the flat surface before the slope. Instead, he attempted to lower the gear while descending the slope which resulted in continuous momentum gain. Due to extreme panic, sudden uncontrollable fear, loss of nerves, and his complete attention towards changing the gear, the driver failed to apply any of the brakes, neither service brakes nor hand brakes. This can be also confirmed by the fact that no brake marks were visible on the right of way where the accident happened. Rough terrain, inclined profile of land and filled water in the bowser contributed in increasing momentum of the descending bowser. Driver did not follow the speed limit, he also did not follow the safe driving practice required for the hilly terrain. Failure to effectively implement required actions for controlling the hazard. The driver tried to direct the bowser towards crown/shoulder of the road to stop the vehicle, which instead lifted the tanker and ultimately it rolled over. Supervisor failed to ensure that every worker should attend TBT before the job begins. Helper was appointed by driver without any prior information or approval. Therefore, helper was missing the basic skill set and orientation required to perform the job.
corrective_actions:
• Company Driving Policy and Safe Driving Practices shall always be followed.
• Vehicle's speed shall always be reduced, and gears should be lowered before descending on slope.
• Speed Limit shall always be followed.
• Driving Techniques shall always be adapted as per the Terrain and surrounding conditions.
• Attendance of all workers shall be ensured in ToolBox Talks (TBTs).
• Hazards associated with workplace and surrounding conditions must be discussed and communicated to workers in all TBTs.

narrative: Two divers were involved in an incident during underwater hull repair project for a Floating Production and Storage & Offloading (FPSO) vessel at an offshore production field. The work was conducted at seat with depth of 6 meters (approximately 20 feet). The divers left a Diving Support Vessel (DSV) to perform an adapter mating test. While positioning the adapter in its intended location, the adapter suddenly lost its buoyancy and sank. One of the divers (Diver 1) was seen sinking together with the adapter to a depth of 55 meters (approximately 180 feet), entangled with the adapter rope. Diver 2 rescued Diver 1 and swam up together with unconscious Diver 1 to the surface. Diver 1 was taken to DSV compression chamber, but had lost vital signs at that point. He was pronounced dead four hours after CPR was attempted to revive him.
what_went_wrong: Deviation from approved procedure (Diving Safety Management System Manual) during diving operation and emergency procedure.
corrective_actions:
• Existing Company Site Representatives (CSR), offshore diving supervisors and superintendent shall complete trainings as per IMCA Client Offshore and IMCA C 003.
• Future SISO involving diving operations to include company standards in Diving Operations Management.

narrative: During rig move and rigging down operations, the drilling crew was dismantling the TDS. The task was to disconnect the TDS from the guide beam by disengaging the tie-back hook pins. Two Floormen were assigned to remove the upper tie-back hook pins while the Derrickman was to remove the lower tie-back hook pins. Three of the four tie-back hook pins were successfully disengaged, and when the Derrickman was detaching the last tie-back hook pin, the TDS skid swung towards the Floorman's (IP 1) position and struck him against the mast beam. IP # 1 sustained fatal chest injuries. Simultaneously, at the rig floor, the Assistant Electrician (IP 2) was working with the Instrumentation Technician to remove and lower the disconnected TDS service loop cables from the rig floor to the ground. While the Instrumentation Technician pushed the cable away from the handrail, the jerking motion accelerated by gravity made the TDS service loop cable hit IP # 2, who was standing nearby, resulting in IP # 2 losing his balance and falling approximately 40 feet to the ground. IP 2 sustained a fatal head injury.
what_went_wrong:
• Inadequate Identification of Worksite Hazard.
• Inadequate Leadership / Supervision.
• In effective Monitoring / Auditing of Safety Process.
corrective_actions:
• PTW authorities must review the PTW and associated documents for adequacy before signatures.
• Review the existing JSA for rigging down TDS to cover the risk of sudden movement of the TDS and implement the revised JSA on rigs having similar TDS.
• Prepare a consolidated list of rig move activities and enhance the Rig Move on Paper (RMOP).
• Enhance the quality of the Integrated Work Activity Planning (IWAP) process by comprehensively planning and scheduling all activities during rig move and include DTMs in the rig move IWAP meetings.
• Adequate and constant supervision is required to ensure safe execution of the task.

narrative: Near miss: Slickline tool dropped. During second run of slickline operations and after setting the lock mandrel in the landing nipple, the contractor operator was in a slickline unit pulling out a toolstring using a joystick handle. • The supervisor was not trained on this AMS system.
• Overconfident.
• Human error.
corrective_actions:

• Slickline service provider to audit that slickline field crews adhere to operational procedures by reviewing job logs retrieved from the unit.
• Pre-set alarms are mandatory prior to start any job to prevent human errors due to over confidence.
• Effective Management of red zone area can prevent serious injuries.

narrative: During a rainy period, a closed drainage valve caused rainwater to accumulate on the roof of a tank that favoured the growth of moss and lichen. There were also traces of paint on the tank roof following recent waterproofing work. A team of operators (T1) had been working on the roof of the tank to clean off the moss and traces of paint. The team was using a presumed algaecide/fungicide considered as a specific, multi-surface, grease-removing agent -and equipment (PPE, scrapers, brooms, etc.). Later, a second team (2), which was working on the tank wall, noticed a paint run in their work area. Because they did not have any cleaning agent, they asked team (1) to give them some of the product. Team (2) took what they thought was an empty metal pot of hardener as a recipient for the cleaning agent, in fact containing a residue of hardener and paint from a previous work - and poured part of the cleaning agent into it. When they had finished their task (around midday), the rest of the product that had not been used (around 3 litres) was handed back to team (1). At the end of the day, the remaining product in the metal pot was poured back into a container of the pure product. Exhausted by the heat, the operators left the work area, leaving the equipment and products on site. In the early evening, two firefighters performing their round noticed smoke coming from the tank roof and stepped in to contain the fire outbreak. The container into which the product had been poured had melted and spontaneously combusted. The fire had then spread to the equipment nearby and damaged part of the separating wall on the periphery of the roof. Immediate actions: -Intervention by firefighters and triggering of the deluge system of the tank.
what_went_wrong:
• Exothermic reaction after chemicals had been mixed (paint +product + hardener) in a closed polyethylene container. Additional causes identified:
• Poor chemical storage management.
• Work area not properly tidied at the end of the shift.
• It was Insufficient maintenance of the rainwater drainage system causing moss to accumulate.
• Insufficient supervision of works and non-compliance with work permit close-out rules.
• Lack of knowledge and awareness of the risks related to the use of chemicals.
• Fatigue due to heat exposure. Conditions not identified during the risk assessment. Process Safety Fundamental: We control ignition sources. We respect hazards.
corrective_actions:
• Check that the operators handling chemicals have received suitable training.
• During safety rounds, check that chemical containers are suitable, properly labelled and stored in areas surrounded by a means of retention.
• Factor in information on chemical compatibility (Ref. Material Safety Data Sheets).
• Remind people of the obligation to clean and tidy the work area when work is finished, preferably when the permit is closed out for the day.
• Check that the tank rainwater drainage valves are open during rainy periods and/or after periods of heavy rainfall.
• Remind team managers about the work permit process.
• Take into account the stress involved in the work and the exposure to intense heat when preparing the work and in the risk assessment.

narrative: During a transfer operation of personnel to the platform boat landing by boat, a wave suddenly appeared and unbalanced the boat. narrative: A crane operator was running the crane to support the construction project team in the installation of the Mobile crane at a Platform. The banksman gave a signal to the crane operator to swing right, he successfully swung right and cleared the brace from the MAST top section. The next signal was given to the crane operator to lift the load (King post brace). what_went_wrong:

• He panicked and inadvertently swung the crane boom to the left and the load abruptly moved above the MAST top section of the King Post, where two employees were positioned on the scaffold.

corrective_actions:

• Signage installed in the crane cabin to remind the operator of the use of the stop pin, and reiterate the importance of fastening the lever to the linkage.
• Field crane operator portfolio needs to be upgraded to include more people.

narrative: On March 16th, a M-8 Helicopter was about to lift a cargo net of 10x200l Fuel Drums at the Base laydown. The load master had connected the cargo net lifting points of the chains, and signalled for the aircraft to lift. As the longline started to become taut the loadmaster started to move away to the safe area and noticed the lifting points of the net dropped with the weight of the chains. When he looked up, he observed the longline falling down in a spiral loop from the aircraft and moved further away to a safe location. The flight engineer advised the captain flying that the hook had released. The captain checked with the load master if he was safe and after confirmation the aircraft returned to the helipad. The 52m longline with load cell (75kg total) came to stop on the ground approximately 7 metres from the load and 6 metres away from the loadmaster. No personnel were injured, and no equipment was damaged.
what_went_wrong:

• Operating in high humidity and high rain fall environment.
• Close proximity of pin 11 to pin 16.
corrective_actions:
• Ensure the maintenance program for parked machines is implemented with checks on critical components.
• Inspect the multiple pin connectors for wet and corrosion tracks during the manufacturers specified 100 hourly service.
• Inspect the hook control line for correct DC power (27V) during the manufacturers specified 100 hourly service.
• Use dehumidifier in aircraft operating in high humidity and rain fall environment when parked.
• Use covers/tarps over cockpit during heavy rain events.
• Ensure that escape routes for the loadmasters are identified and free of obstacles.
• Ensure that the laydown area is free of non-essential personnel.

narrative: At approximately 16:00 hrs, the operation was stand by on the weather at the shelter area. A Bosun, an Able Seaman (AB) and a cadet were transferring equipment from the ship's office to the ship's garage under the crane along the ship's safe walkway. They observed that the ladder that had previously been secured to the ship's side railing started to become loose and they went out of the safe zone walkway to the side railing to re-secure the steps. At this time there were heavy swells coming past the vessel but they did not observe any coming over the side as they watched for a few minutes. While they started to re-secure the steps and had taken their eyes off the incoming sea, a large swell around 3 - 4m came over the side of the bulwarks of the vessel and hit the ABs (IP). The swell was strong enough for him to lose his footing and he fell on the deck and was pushed down the deck to just forward of the crane pedestal. The Bosun and Cadet came to assist the IP who was unable to get back up due to an injury to his ankles. The IP was carried by stretcher to the sick bay where the IP was assessed by the medic. The Incident happened very quickly, and there is no evidence to show exactly what has caused the injuries to the IP.
what_went_wrong: Pressure from swell knocked IP down.
corrective_actions: Not available.

narrative: An operations team were preparing a 14" pipeline riser for reconnection to a new topside facility service with the cap suitable for the associated axial load. The 14" condensate export line had remained isolated, water-filled, inhibited, and decommissioned since the project hook down phase in 2019. The line was positively isolated at one end and fitted with an engineered cap at the other end. The cap was connected to the riser via a pipe coupling. Both cap and coupling were rated for 10bar service with the cap suitable for the associated axial load. As 100% lower exposure limit was identified when sampling the void space contents at one end, as per local procedure, the team were attempting to perform Nitrogen pressure purges of the 10-metre void space to displace residual hydrocarbon before removal of the cap to allow welding of a connecting pup-spool to the open riser. Whilst trying to locally verify the applied N2 purge pressure, the engineered cap and pipe coupling were vertically ejected. The equipment and debris resulted in physical injuries to three people in the vicinity; Injured Person 1 was lifted upward and fell back to scaffold, Injured persons 2 and 3 suffered minor facial injuries from impact with debris and/or equipment.
what_went_wrong:
• Applied N2 purge pressure exceeded axial strength of pipe coupling.
- Improper installation of coupling during hook down, invalidated pressure rating of assembly.
• Uncertainty of pressure applied due to use of ineffective purge equipment (wrong pressure indicator range, no overpressure protection, inadequate control of pressure).
• Multiple workers in vicinity of work site.
- Access to work site not controlled (no barriers).
- Failure to mitigate Line of Fire hazard (N2 manifold locally mounted at riser location).
• Purging proceeded without stopping job.
- Recognized concerns did not lead to an effective intervention.
• •Inadequate Pipeline/Process integrity assurance process.
- Installation of 10bar coupling during hook down did not lead to formal derating of pipeline.
- Poor installation and lack of 'mechanical completion' checks at hook down
- Operational hook-up needs not fully considered at hook down phase. Process Safety Fundamental: We apply procedures. We stop if the unexpected occurs.
corrective_actions:
• Ensure that process/pipeline integrity is maintained for temporarily decommissioned lines and equipment (de-rating, testing, verification, recording and assurance).
• Ensure that site procedures provide adequate mitigation of risks associated with N2 purging activities, and that overpressure protection, system integrity check, and correct means of pressure control/monitoring are assured as prerequisite controls.
• Ensure that purge and/or pressure test equipment is located to mitigate line of fire hazard.
• Ensure that pressure purging activities are regarded as high-risk, and systematically subjected to method statement, risk assessment and PTW.

narrative: The oil export pump shaft started to rotate while personnel was working up close to the shaft. The work, adjusting a sensor, had just ended when the shaft started to turn. The rotation of the shaft was caused by the starting of the upstream oil booster pump. This caused the fluid in the line from the booster pump to turn the impeller on the export pump B, causing the shaft to spin. This could happen as there was no mechanical isolation of the oil export pump.
what_went_wrong:
• There was no mechanical isolation of the oil export pump.
• Lack of coordination of simultaneous activities.
• The description of the job was added to an approved PTW.
• Perceived time shortage.
corrective_actions:
Improve the work permit (WP) process based on lessons learned from projects that have used it.
• Make sure that the greenfield WP process is improved based on experiences from all projects that have used the process.
• Bring in more focus on mechanical isolation for work on rotating equipment. Define requirements to mechanical isolation according to requirements to electrical isolation.
• Set stricter requirements on how to use a general WP, including defining a general WP.
• Set requirements to use the brownfield WP process for pressurized and energized mechanical systems, not only when HC is present.
• When the scope is changed after WP has been approved, the WP should be reapproved. This should be considered as a point/requirement in the WP process.
• Improve quality in WP descriptions and be compliant to the requirements. Description and attachment to the WP. It shall be possible to understand the task and the corresponding risk to each task in a WP.

• Work should be stopped for reassessment whenever conditions change.

narrative: An 80 ton crane and operator had completed a lifting operation at the production facility for the installation of a new security cabin, and were due to return to the town, when the driver received a call from the crane owner requiring him to relocate both himself and the crane to a well inside our operation block, due to a hose leak identified on an existing crane at the rig site (another crane used at rig site). On route, the crane's brakes started to smoke due to the steep decline from the well site road turning to the base of the mountain, where the driver stopped to let the brakes cool down for approximately 33 minutes. The driver then restarted the crane and continued his journey. The route was a total distance of 31.2 kilometres. The first stop was after 3.1 kilometres calculated from the wellsite turning to the base of the mountain due to the crane's brakes starting to smoke. The driver continued his journey a further 26.1 kilometres over inclining and declining roads before approaching the turning. As the driver reached the turning, he found that the brakes would not function and that the crane was moving too fast to make the right turn. A split-second decision was made to continue down the declining road hoping that the road would level out. The crane driver was unaware that the well site was located 2 kilometres ahead at the bottom of the hill. On approach to the well site, the crane crashed through both the security barrier and perimeter gates, continued across the pad, colliding with two concrete barriers used to protect the flowline, before finally coming to a stop above the flowline after pushing the line off its supporting brackets.
what_went_wrong: Immediate Cause: Brake failure due to an incorrectly set up braking system reducing the crane's braking power to less than 40%. Basic Cause: The sub-standard setup of the crane's braking system on August 6 and 7 meant that only three of its eight wheels were fully functional, severely reducing its stopping power. The crane driver did not hold a driving license, heavy plant license or crane training certificate. Root Cause: No contractor assurance systems in place pre/post contract award. A system for auditing and inspecting contractors and sub-contractors would assure that compliance with contractual obligations is being fulfilled before contract award and throughout the contract's lifetime. Process Safety Fundamental: We stop if the unexpected occurs.
corrective_actions:
• Implementing third-party audits and inspections of contractors and sub-contractors confirms contractual and legal compliance in line with a suitable standard, such as ISO 9001. This program would need to include pre-contract and post-contract awards.
• Enhance operational controls to include inspections of driver's licenses with specific attention to driving categories.
• Assessment of security checkpoints confirming suitability of controls.
• Company to consider the contract hire of a full-time 80Ton crane and two crane operators on a rotational basis. Hiring a crane and operator would significantly reduce the need to hire cranes externally while ensuring compliance with Local and National Laws.

narrative: The secondary roof (25m x 9.5m) of the newly constructed laundry building became detached due to extreme high winds, traveling approximately 50m, before landing on the main camp generators, resulting in a minor diesel spill (diesel leak contained within bund and therefore not categorized as a spill).
what_went_wrong:
The Roofing Subcontractor:
• failed to follow manufacturer's drawings and procedures.
• failed to use 5x38 fixings to anchor the canopy to the laundry building chassis.
• used tack welds as an alternative/unapproved method of joining the structures together. High wind speeds of up to 78.6km created the energy to lift the canopy structure from the building.
corrective_actions:
• Contractor Selection and Oversight - Contractor pre-qualification process not effective: a pre-qualification process was in place and utilized, but it did not identify relevant deficiencies in the Contractor's capabilities.
• Subcontractor Management - Lack of control by the Principal Contractor, who mobilized a roofing subcontractor without performing competence verification or due diligence checks.
• Inadequate work oversight (company/contractor) - Company had limited resources to cover the Camp Construction activities. Main contractor failed to provide proper oversight of the Subcontractor's work activities.

• Formalise communication between company and contractor- written Procedures should be developed for operational phase and communication numbers to be shared.

• Ensure all surrounding handrails are checked and discussed during Toolbox talk prior starting new job. Concerned JSA to be updated.
• Maintain handrails register up to date with established preventative maintenance system.
• Implement annual third-party handrail inspection and testing.

narrative: During rig out of the service rig, a worker was attempting to coil and stow a temporary electrical cable. The cable end became stuck underneath the catwalk. The workers right hand (with donned wet glove) made contact with the inner connections (4 pole/208 Volts/60 Amps). The worker reported experiencing a momentary electrical shock. The ground conditions were snow covered with water accumulation in low spots atop frozen ground with temperatures of +5 Degrees Celsius with clear skies.

• All electrical panels on service rigs must have the "Plug End" connection. The power cord must have the "Socket End" part of the connection.
• There needs to be a physical lock and LOTO procedure for power cord at the rig electrical panel. Admin Controls: There is a need to create a Work Instruction for energy isolation, installation/removal and securement of the service rig powered systems. Contractor HSSE Management: Expectations shall be set for Contractors to provide their audit plan/schedule, and to review results/insights at appropriate frequency.

narrative: A rig contractor was rigging down from a well, and the logistics contractor was in the process of removing the V-door from the substructure. The lifting equipment was secured, with a tagline attached. Pins securing the V door to the substructure were removed to allow lifting and removal of the V-door. As the load was being lifted, the crane reversed, and the load levelled. This created a bind in the load, causing one of the d-rings to dislodge from the lifting hook. The V-door fell approximately 3 metres onto the drill line and managed pressure drilling line below. All personnel were clear of the area at the time of the event, and no injuries were reported.
what_went_wrong:
Inadequate supervision:
• Supervisory personnel did not ensure crane inspection was conducted prior to the mechanical lift.
• Supervisory personnel did not ensure rigging equipment was adequate for the task.
• Onsite supervision failed to identify and properly manage onsite operational hazards and risks. Deviation from Procedures by Crew:
• Onsite personnel did not follow proper lifting best practices. Inadequate Hazard Identification:
• Onsite personnel failed to identify and properly manage mechanical lifting risks.
corrective_actions:
• Survey of Reiteration of Policy/Procedure Utilization: Management of the contractor reiterated to personnel the existing procedures for Crane lifting operations and confirm personnel understand how to apply these procedures.
• Equipment Replacement: Contractor personnel replaced the latch on the lifting hook and implemented additional (4 leg chain sling) to avoid improper lifting angles caused by load levelling.
• Post Incident Toolbox Talk and Sharing Lessons Learned: Shortly following the incident, onsite meeting was held with teams from both company and contractors. Event was discussed in detail to fully understand causes, inadequacies, and where utilization of procedures and safe work practices need to be applied to prevent reoccurrence. Expectation of following established mechanical lifting procedures was re-emphasized.
• Crane Inspection: Daily crane inspection conducted and documented prior to resuming operations.
• Retraining Recommendation: Company requested contractor to conduct refresher training to its personnel in identifying, assessing, and mitigating hazards/risks as they apply to specific operations.

narrative: During a period of high winds, the wellsite sign became dislodged from the securing frame from which it was mounted on the antenna deck and fell to the deck below. There were no personnel in the area at the time; no other equipment was damaged. The 73lb. sign fell 15 feet, registering as high potential on the DROPS calculator.
what_went_wrong: While preparing for an operation, the vessel was positioned to where high winds created optimal conditions to apply pressure to the sign. Additionally, securing hardware was present only around the edges of the sign, and its placement was in a location that provided better visibility and access but left it vulnerable to wind conditions.
corrective_actions: The combination of the frame design along with the hardware used was not adequate to ensure the sign was secured. The sign was constructed of thin sheet metal which is more vulnerable to wind effects and letters were secured by small wing nuts which present multiple hazards. The design also required two crew members to lift the sign up and over a handrail to change information.

narrative: While rigging up elevators to 16 foot bails in preparation of the 7 5/8 inch casing pull, the link tilt was kicked out away from well centre by inflating the link tilt air bag to install the secondary safety latch sensor on the elevators. The link tilt air bag ruptured resulting in the 16 foot bails coming to rest on the rig floor. A worker was tasked with installing the safety latch sensor and was positioned in between the elevators and the 7 5/8 inch casing stump. The casing elevators contacted the worker's right shin.
what_went_wrong: When 16 foot bails are kicked out past the stops using the link tilt system, most equipment configurations will create a strain on the system that is beyond the rated capacity of the air bags. The safety latch sensor was installed by the IP in a body position that created a line of fire risk.
corrective_actions:
• The link tilt system was a pneumatic design which functioned by inflating the air bag. Other locations utilized a hydraulic link tilt with a greater operational capacity.
• The link tilt air bag was viewed as an expendable part. Previous failures were not recognized to have an HSE risk, and therefore, not investigated.
• Replacement parts were ordered through the rig contractor equipment acquisition process which does not interface with the Company inventory, inspection, and maintenance system. The operational life & parameters, and inspection & maintenance criteria for parts ordered this way are not tracked.
• An MOC was routed for an upgrade to a different casing elevator, however, the impact of this change was not fully understood - the new elevators require 16 foot bails which are too heavy for the link tilt air bag according to the load chart.
• To save time with the installation of the secondary safety latch sensor on the casing elevators, a deviation from the approved method of installation was made. The service provider trains personnel to install these sensors with the elevators placed on the ground, however, since the bails were already kicked out away from well-centre, the decision was made in the moment to complete the install with the system raised.

narrative: During test activities with the PTS pump in a Pulling Rig, the person operating the machine detected that the lever brake system of the hoist did not fully respond and carried out 2 strokes using the equipment's socket/clutch to stop the downward movement. This situation was observed by the Company Man who ordered to stop the task. In order to stop the task and leave the equipment in a safe condition, the operator decided to raise the pipe as much as possible to avoid leaving the pump resting on the bottom and place the pneumatic wedges. As it rose, it reached the end of the stroke, causing the hoist to fall, reaching the bottom, resting on its side and bending the tubing.
what_went_wrong:
• Use of defective equipment: continuity of operation despite detecting failure in brakes.
• Lack of competence: machinist operator not qualified for the function.
• Inadequate work standard: it is not defined from what degree of lack of brake regulation the manoeuvre must be stopped. There is no instruction that defines the unsafe condition.
corrective_actions:
• Place a physical indicator next to the brake lever that indicates the adjustment range at a glance.
• Develop a training plan for greater function in pulling and flushby teams.
• Reinforce training in the identification of critical security elements.
• Generate specific instructions on regulation and checking of the brake system.

narrative: During the monthly/weekly inspection of the lifeboats and the rescue boat (scope of the preventive maintenance program), in the test of the descent brake of the rescue boat, the davit winch cable broke and the boat fell into the sea from an approximate height of 20 metres. The test consists of releasing the boat with braking after approximately 5 metres of descent by gravity. When braking, the cable broke. The boat was unmanned, as per the test procedure. There was no risk of hitting people. There was no rupture of fuel or lubricant tanks.
what_went_wrong:
• Test execution with descent speed higher than specified in the manufacturer's manual and IMO.
• Dynamic brake failure to maintain the design speed.
corrective_actions:
• Evaluate the inclusion of a task to measure the descent speed of the rescue boat with a frequency of less than 5 years.
• Apply the compliance with the Procedure Verification tool to verify that the procedures for operating safeguard equipment are adequate and that they are being complied with.

narrative: After replacing the oxygen cylinder of the oxyacetylene set, when the worker opened the cylinder valve, there was an abrupt increase in pressure. At that moment, the pressure regulator and flame arrester could not withstand this sudden increase, causing a burst and spring projection against the workshop wall. The worker was not hit, due to his position on the opposite side of the projection.
what_went_wrong:
• Maintenance failure: cylinders reconfirmed without internal cleaning control and procedures.
• Maintenance failure: no maintenance plan on the pressure regulator.
• Procedure failure: the procedure did not provide for a welding service with an oxyacetylene set.
• Human Factors (behavioural): lack of attention, stress, worry, etc.
corrective_actions:
• Request the periodic inspection certificate and the product analysis certificate from the oxygen cylinder supplier.
• Create a maintenance plan for pressure regulators.
• Review the contracted company's procedure, including the activities and risk analysis of the oxyacetylene welding process.
• Carry out training with the entire team involved and demonstrate it with an attendance list.

narrative: During maintenance work on a 3" automatic valve, located at the NGL outlet of a condensate stabilizer (on standby) there was a leak of condensed liquid. During the event, there was no damage to people or assets. This event was classified as a Tier 2 PSE.
what_went_wrong:
PERSONAL FACTORS
• Lack of risk awareness. There was no evidence of the task ́s planning/scope process performed by either the planner or the operator. During planning, it is not detected that the valve to be intervened does not have blocking valves.
• Inadequate discipline. Work Permit with an isolation certificate that does not correspond. The lack of adequate isolation certificate is not detected neither by operator nor by local area authority. LABOR / SYSTEM FACTORS
• Inadequate work scheduling/planning. The planning/scope process was performed by either the planner or the operator.
• Normalization of deviation from a procedure. Upon the change in the scope of the task, the local area authority nor the operator required to suspend the task and renew the ATS.
• Inadequate identification of risks in the design. Valve to intervene does not have blocking valves.
• Inadequate assessment of preventive maintenance needs. The preventive maintenance program is not executed. Process Safety Fundamentals: We maintain safe isolation. We respect hazards.
corrective_actions:
• Carry out reinforcement training in compliance with the Life Saving Rules.
• Ensure that Contractors maintenance personnel have the appropriate competence for the work to be carried out in the plant.
• Carry out training campaigns on hazards and risk of the plant process and Stop the Job Policy for maintenance personnel.
• Design control valve maintenance strategy.

narrative: During river water filling operation of tank, there was a loss of containment in the walls of the riveted tank, causing the tank to collapse.
what_went_wrong:
PERSONAL FACTORS
• Inadequate discipline. Normalization of the tank overfill deviation. LABOR FACTORS
• Inadequate Management of Change. Change of service of the tank / No evidence of MoC for the dosing of chemicals to the water. The design of the tank was not verified when it was incorporated into the operation. Tank does not meet the applicable manufacturing standard for this service. The risk of changing the density of the water due to the accumulation of solids inside the tank was not identified.
• Inadequate assessment of preventive maintenance needs. There is no preventive maintenance program and no critical evaluation registered in company system for the asset. Equipment was not available for inspection.
• Lack of supervision. Normalization of deviation. The tank ́s condition as rejected was not kept after the Integrity inspection; the defective equipment was operated; tank repair was not prioritized.
• Inadequate assessment of needs and risks. The tank is not registered as a safety critical element and does not have a criticality analysis in the company system.
• Inadequate work procedure. There was no specific procedure or limits defined for the filling operation of the tank.
corrective_actions:
• Ensure the correct execution of preventive maintenance programs.
• Ensure the availability of equipment when requested for scheduled maintenance.
• Report instrument control and safety systems failures.
• Ensure management of change when tanks are assigned for a new use other than the one for which it was designed.

narrative: After completion of activities under the scope of a preventive maintenance on Deck Crane B, an employee was preparing to lower materials from the top of the crane. At the beginning of the descent movement, when the set was at the crane's upper platform level, it bumped at its guardrail and the knot came loose and the materials fell to the Main Deck, which had not been barriered-off for this crane maintenance. The location of the Main Deck where the objects hit was close to an escape route, being an area of regular and frequent passing of people. what_went_wrong:

corrective_actions:

• Reinforce the improvement of isolation barriers around possible area of impact of falling objects in all teams.
• Remove all ropes stored in the crane that are used to lift manual tools/equipment. All manual tools or equipment to be used in any maintenance work at the crane to be transferred in adequate tool bag.
• Reinforce the use of 'Drops prevention' tools to perform any approved work when there is a risk of falling objects above 2 metres and properly secure tools and equipment when there is a need to transfer them up/down the unit levels. Confirm that control of "drops prevention' tools are in place, i.e.: logbook, to minimise the risk of potential dropped object.

narrative: On 15/06/2022 during the night shift at about 23h00, during POOH, ESP completion, the Operator was in the Rig floor adjusting the spider handling tool to get it back onto its normal working position. what_went_wrong: Lack of communication: IP was still centring the load with his hands. narrative: On 26 March 2022, A scaffolder, working on a gas development, suffered a serious finger injury during operations to de-construct a scaffold tower. A colleague of the injured scaffolder was lowering the scaffold board from a platform at 17m elevation (1) to another colleague on the level below (2) when the scaffold board slipped from his grasp and fell. • Numerous opportunities to intervene were missed.

1. The injury to the IP occurred during a standard activity which was not under any abnormal conditions. The action of pulling on a spanner to undo a nut that was not excessively tight may have occurred during any other routine manual task.
2. The use of a battery impact driver to undo the bolts was not achievable as there is only 130mm clearance between the top of the bolt and the bottom of the cattle grid. A retrofit option was introduced on two of the bolts where a 25mm hole was drilled through the cattle grid frame to allow the impact driver to be used. This method was not practical for undoing all the mounting bolts as the bolts could be undone by hand in approximately the same time and with minimal effort.
3. There is a less labour-intensive way to conduct this task which involves less manual labour (jet blaster/vac truck). However, this method presents its own difficulties and hazards (wearing a face shield) as stated by the contractor and they ceased performing the task.
4. The lack of maintenance increases sand compaction levels in the grid making either method of cleaning the grid more difficult than is necessary i.e., non-compacted sand would require minimal or no water blasting preventing the issue with the face mask being worn and also making the grid easier to remove using the alternative method.
5. The criticality level of cleaning the cattle grids have a 'very low' priority ranking on the Work Prioritisation Matrix. If a work order to clean a grid does make it to the work schedule, it is often postponed or removed due to a lack of resourcing to perform the task.
corrective_actions:
1. narrative: A crew member was injured while attempting to secure cargo on deck. Crew members were working to secure cargo with chains and binders. The water washing over the stern was pushing a cargo container towards the IP, which struck the IP's lower right leg causing a fracture and leading to permanent reduction of musculoskeletal function.
what_went_wrong:
The following were identified as causes of the incidents:
• Unsecured cargo during paused transfer operations with deteriorating weather conditions. The conditions that led to the incident resulted from the combination of poor weather conditions, orientation of the vessel in the path of wave action during the activity of re-securing loose cargo.
• Incremental creep, while on its own did not appear to have resulted in material changes, resulted in an overall higher cumulative.
corrective_actions:
• Minimizing the amount of loose cargo and the amount of time cargo remains unsecured, add additional protection to keep cargo in place if rough conditions are experienced.

narrative: Engine boy performed a routine visual check of the engine room of the vessel to support geophysical activity. At one point, a possible oil leak was identified in one of the starboard generator filters. The worker then positioned himself between the bulkhead (wall) of the engine room and the generator, so that he could have a better view of the filter, where the leak supposedly occurred. While he was in that position, the vessel moved suddenly due to the sea conditions. The worker lost his balance and, to avoid falling, tried to hold on, involuntarily placing his hand on the pulley of the water pump that was in operation, suffering amputation of the distal phalanx of the fourth finger of his left hand.
what_went_wrong:
• There are no plans and procedures for inspection, testing, and maintenance: documentary evidence demonstrating that the maintenance system was not fully implemented on the vessel.
• Ambiguous or confusing instructions and requirements: the existing procedure for the inspection activity (round) in the engine room does not provide it's definition and does not establish the limits between inspection and maintenance, that is, when the activity ceases to be inspection and becomes maintenance.
• Errors are not detectable: workers reported carrying out these inspection activities in the same way, several times a day, for many years, with Normalization of Deviance for the inspection activity.
• Failure to ensure the performance of activities in accordance with established requirements: employee proactivity, seeking to act for the benefit of the company to carry out a procedure different from the one he was performing (inspection).
• Conflicting layouts: reduced spaces depending on the size of the vessel, the environment presents unevenness, noise, presence of heat, vibration, no visibility to the external environment and no bulkheads and supports suitable for this purpose, which makes it difficult to carry out activities.
• Inadequate environmental conditions: easy access to unprotected and poorly marked dangerous locations and partial protection of moving parts in the Generator Motor Group.
• Did not consider the reduction of human exposure to the consequences of possible equipment or system failures: a crew member went to carry out an intervention on the Motor Generator Group oil filter, due to a possible leak.
• Inadequate monitoring: unmanned machine room, without telemetry and automation indicators/controls in the Motor Generator Group.
• Inadequate control measures: lack of protection on the internal part of the water pump pulley of the Motor Generator Group.
• Natural phenomenon: vessel hit by a beam wave. Met oceanographic conditions with 2m waves were considered normal for activity. The day before, a rough sea (storm) warning had been issued for the area.
• Short deadline for carrying out the task: pre-operational phase of the activity demands intense interaction between the Company HSE team and the Contractor and there is little time between the vessel availability for initial inspections and the start of the project. HSE teams need to carry out inspections in a short time and without operations actually taking place.
corrective_actions:
Lessons learnt:
• Work on sizing HSE teams to better support operations.
• Improve the inspection system for contractors regarding the release of vessels to begin activities.
• Review emergency communication flows between the Contractor and Company, for greater agility in responding to accident victims.
• Strengthen inspection demands from contractors to remedy deficiencies in the implementation of HSE recommendations identified by contractors or by the company HSE team. Recommendations:
• Complete the implementation of the onboard maintenance system.
• Review the procedure, detailing the inspection activity (round), providing its definition, establishing its limits, (inspection versus maintenance) and ensuring training of the workforce in this procedure, including onboard leaders.
• Carry out a study to understand the current company culture and propose solutions to combat the normalization of deviations, preferably supported by human factors concepts, using the Company human factors guidelines.
• Conduct human factors training with senior leadership and crews, using Company human factors guidelines: Trust is fundamental; People create security; How we respond to failure matters a lot; Learning and improving is key to success; and context directs behaviour, so that workers are able to understand internal and external forces, such as cultural and organizational issues, that interfere with daily activities.
• Carry out an ergonomic study of the vessel engine room to identify risks, propose the necessary control measures and improvements.
• Protect and signal dangerous locations and unprotected moving parts in the Motor Generator Group, as well as in other equipment in the engine room.
• Improve the reliability of machines, equipment and components in the engine room.
• Carry out a study to verify the possibility of equipping the engine room with indicators, telemetry controls and/or automation.
• Protect and mark the water pump pulley of the Motor Generator Group.
• Define and implement the operational limits of met oceanographic conditions for each activity on the vessel.

narrative: The activity on well 2 started on June 17th with the equipment mobilization in location. On June 18th the job officially commenced on site. The Scope of Work was to carry out maintenance activities on Xmas Tree and ambient valve recalibration. Operation was performed with support of Slick Line service and downhole plug. During the activity, the team observed the Slick Line and the upper sheave were not moving. In order to fix the issue, the Contractor Supervisor bled off the pressure in the hydraulic hose of the SL stuffing box through the dedicated hydraulic line, and proceeded to slack the cable at the bottom sheave to resume jar action This brought to failure the pressure equalization across the downhole plug and consequently led to the ejection of the same inside the lubricator which parted and jumped on air. The lubricator ejection determined the Slick Line cable tension and strong knockback. Consequently,the lower sheave, connected to such cable, strongly impacted the IP's chest and chin. IP medical conditions immediately appeared critical. The event led also to a slight gas release.
what_went_wrong:
• Rigless Programme developed PtW, Risk Assessment, Method of Statement, Isolation Certificate, TBT forms: all available in location, improvement needs have been observed in the procedures coordination and implementation.
• Lack of supervision.
• In presence of an issue (blocked Slick Line sheave), Contractor Supervisor decided to bleed off pressure in the hydraulic hose of the Slick Line stuffing box by pushing the small ball in the check valve seat allowing the hydraulic oil to bleed. This brought to the failure of the pressure equalization and following lubricator's ejection. Operator did not stop the activity to re-assess the Risks.
• The Contractor's personnel competences were not previously assessed before starting the activity due to lack of Procedures. During the contractor's personnel interviews carried out in the Investigation process, competence's gaps appeared evident for some crew members.
• Lack of knowledge on First Aid Operations and Emergency Communications. Night MEDEVAC Operations to be improved.
corrective_actions:
• While dealing with high pressure fluids, ensure proper barriers always in place.
• In case the assessed workflow (as per method of statement) changes, proper risk assessment must be done and mitigations identified. It must be treated as management of change.
• Whenever you are planning a job, always take into consideration the operational context and the process conditions.
• All operations (routine and critical ones) require competent person to be performed; their knowledge must be formally assessed prior to start any job.
• In all locations medevac drills must be performed and personnel to be adequately informed and trained about the existent procedures to be implemented.
• Proper communication devices in remote areas are fundamental to manage any emergency situation.
• Ensure safe rescue by medevac of the workers during day & night.
• Stop work authority to be always applied whenever required (anyone is entitled).

narrative: A high potential event occurred when unbolting a pressurized flange. During the assembly and disassembly of blind flanges of the cold box bypass, the GTP performing crew were mistaken about bypass flanges pass A 18" and worked on the blind flanges of pass B which were not already isolated and were under nitrogen pressure. When the crew observed a pressure release, they stopped working and left the area. Afterwards, the exploitation operator was in the area, recognized the situation, and quickly opened the vent to depressurize the line.
what_went_wrong:
• inadequate planning/risk assessment/preparation/supervision
• permit not specific without details
• toolbox talk content unknown and ineffective Supervisor absence: job supervisor did not pause work to confirm the next flange to replace with the area operator. Actual/potential consequences, causes, and actions: So far, the causes identified are ineffective permit system and ineffective supervision:
• no task description available (e.g., job step description), tags were not listed
• permit with vague description approved, HSE revalidation was not marked
• toolbox talk was not documented, content of discussion unknown
• no toolbox talk after lunch break
• the supervisor chose to work on the flange under pressure without confirming with the area operator
corrective_actions:
• Perform a gap analysis on the system to improve the quality, communication, and compliance of the permit to work process.
• Create an improvement action plan that is endorsed by management. Immediate recommendations for short term:
• Attend most permit to work (PTW) meetings to improve quality.
• PTW job description to be clear and work location identified.
• Breaking containment: operator to identify location and prove that the system does not contain pressure nor inventory (e.g., hydrocarbons, chemicals) by opening drains and vents, witnessed by the work team.
• Crew change: relevant incoming staff to countersign permits to ensure they are aware of the activities.
• Permits to be checked for:
- quality of job description
- job steps available
- RA specific for the job
- documented specific risks and controls on toolbox talk (TBT) for the job (or job steps if needed)
- TBT to be held at start of work, after breaks, and when new job steps are added
- TBT to be dated and signed by toolbox (TB) lead
• Late permits to be challenged and scheduled for later if not urgent*
* urgent: having an immediate impact on safety or immediate severe impact on quality or quantity of gas export

narrative: A Hydraulic workover unit (HWU) that was rigged up on top of wellhead fell 49 feet to the ground with 3 workers in the work basket.
what_went_wrong:
The HWU tilted from its vertical axis and fell due to the following causes:
• The casing-wellhead connection strength was greater than the total installed weight on the casing.
• The casing head housing thread had a defect in its threading pre-installation.
• The defect in the casing head threading prevented the complete make-up of the casing head housing threads to the casing pin thread. The casing pin threading had a fracture after installation.
• The casing pin threading fracture reduced the yield strength of the casing-wellhead connection.
• The wellhead collar threading disengaged from the casing threading causing the unit to fall.
corrective_actions: Need to identify any underlying issues in the casing and wellhead prior to activity.

narrative: At 4:42 pm, as a company rental vehicle was returning to the hotel after purchasing supplies for next day lunch boxes, the driver swerved to miss a child riding a bike. The vehicle left the road, hit a power pole, and rolled over twice before coming to rest on the side of the vehicle. The vehicle's speed immediately prior to the incident was recorded at 106 km/h by the IVMS. The maximum speed limit is 60 km/h. The driver and passenger (member of the public) were picked up by a company vehicle soon after the incident, travelling in the opposite direction and taken to the hospital. Both the driver and his passenger were discharged from hospital 3 hours later with no significant injuries reported. Company driver was on duty (but had been on standby) on the day of this incident which was due to low JMP activity.
what_went_wrong: Excessive speed: The primary immediate cause of the incident was the vehicle's speed, recorded at 106 km/h, significantly exceeding the maximum speed limit of 60 km/h. This reckless driving behaviour greatly increased the risk of loss of control and collision. Failure to obtain permission: The driver departed from the hotel premises without obtaining permission. This unauthorized departure deviated from established procedures and compromised the accountability and oversight necessary for safe operations. Unauthorized passenger: Another critical deviation was the driver's unauthorized act of allowing a third-party passenger into the company vehicle. This not only violated company policies but also introduced an additional distraction and potential safety hazard. Non-compliance with seatbelt policy: The failure to enforce the wearing of seatbelts by both the driver and the passenger significantly increased the risk of injury and compromised occupant safety. Lack of adherence to security procedures: The driver did not follow security procedures, particularly those outlined in the journey management plan (JMP). By deviating from established protocols, the driver compromised safety and security measures designed to mitigate risks.
corrective_actions:
• Reinforcing the importance of strict compliance with company policies and Driving - Life Saving Rule.
• Ensure that all passengers are wearing seatbelts before journey starts.
• Check that vehicles are thoroughly inspected before rental and prior to departing on all journeys, and that all reported defects are addressed.
• Consistent monitoring of IVMS data and prompt intervention when deviations are detected.
• Produce in-vehicle rules stickers and SOP for drivers.
• Drivers are not allowed to pick up any un-authorized passengers from outside of the organization.
• Driver shall obtain clearance from Security department prior to departure and provide regular progress updates.
• Update journey management plans and LTMS regarding vehicle age limits.
• Implement driver check tests to be carried out throughout the project.
• After training in defensive driving, carry out refresher training after 6 months.

narrative: One section of a large pipe clamp was found lying on the deck of Module 40, between heating medium circulation pumps B and C. Further assessment confirmed that the clamp had fallen from the discharge line of heating medium circulation pump B. The clamp fell from an estimated 6 metres, and weighed 9.5kg.
what_went_wrong:
• Failure to secure, check, and monitor: two clamps of the heating medium pump B discharge line were not properly installed, and this led to their gradual loosening.
• Sudden temperature variations: the temperature of the pipeline from which the clamp section detached can vary from ambient to 120oC.
• Continuous vibration: the pipeline from which the clamp fell is located close to pieces of equipment which produce vibration, and this led to a gradual and unobvious loosening of the nuts and then the associated bolt.
• Nuts not properly tightened: the nuts of the affected clamp and the second one installed only a few centimetres away were probably not tightened enough.
• Installation of the bolts: the orientation of the bolts allowed the clamp section to drop following the nuts detachment.
• Management systems failed to identify the risk (missing nuts) in time to prevent the incident.
corrective_actions:
• Conduct full Dropped Objects Prevention Scheme (DROPS) sweeps on the topside modules, involving rope access.
• Consider modifying the DROPS inspection schedule so that it more exactly and strictly defines the requirement that meets industry standards. Communicate updated schedule to all affected personnel. Consider implementing audits or assessments to check that the inspection schedule is being followed.
• Conduct engineering study of the different types of clamp design/installation and recommend the most effective design/installation for the heating medium pumps lines.

narrative: Whilst disconnecting a section of hydraulic tubing from a valve actuator, the tubing was inadvertently released under pressure and came into contact with the IP, who was in the line of fire. IP sustained laceration to the right cheek and nose. The job was stopped, and the IP was escorted to the onboard medic. After onboard medical assessment, the IP was sent onshore for further treatment (Medevac).
what_went_wrong: The changing out of the O-ring on the leaking joint on the SDV was not well planned. A permit was not in place to cover the entire O-ring changeout scope, which would have included tubing disconnection. This resulted in the failure to properly assess the overall scope and ensure all risks for the scope were identified and mitigated. The job was only communicated to a few directly involved project team members, and not to relevant stakeholders, such as the Area Authority or Production Superintendent. As a result, the required Control of Work (CoW) authorities were not aware of the scope and therefore unable to validate that appropriate risk controls were in place. This failure is underscored by the lack of adequate coordination between the projects and operations team, which would have fostered an enhanced team approach to project execution. IP was only focused on giving assistance, and failed to enquire on the task ongoing. This resulted in him poorly judging the situation by only concentrating on catching potential oil drips into the bucket he decided to assist in holding, resulting in him placing himself in the line of fire.
corrective_actions:
• Conduct lessons learned sessions covering all crew members, highlighting the potential consequences of misuse of the PTW system, based on this incident.

narrative: While a scaffold supervisor was inspecting/assessing hard barriers at upper levels, a corroded guardrail was seen lying on the grating deck at Upper level 2, beneath CM/SW Exchanger-C cooling medium outlet line and seawater inlet line. The nature of the drop that could have led to its unusual positioning on the grating beneath the pipes on the lower deck was undetermined. The weight of the guardrail was estimated to be 22kg and the mezzanine deck was approximately 3.4 metres from 5P upper level 2. There were no injuries or environmental harm as a result of this incident.
what_went_wrong:

• Cause and type of corrosion identified: after the incident, inspection of the failed base of the handrail was conducted which revealed extensive corrosion at the welded base. Historical leak of seawater from the GRE line onto the handrail structures which was situated directly below it.

corrective_actions:
• Conduct a survey and identify handrails on topsides, with single point of attachments that are subjected to excessive vibration, LSW, and corrosion.

narrative: A tanker approached the pilot boarding area and a fast crew boat arrived to perform the tanker clearance. The tanker had a combination ladder arrangement consisting of a pilot ladder and an accommodation ladder. The terminal pilot along with 3 other people successfully climbed up the pilot ladder before it was the turn of the IP (a terminal agent). A few steps before reaching the accommodation ladder, the IP was feeling exhausted and uncomfortable and started descending back to the fast crew boat. On his way down, he lost his grip of the pilot ladder and fell into the sea with the crew boat being clear from his fall. His life jacket inflated on contact with the sea and he was rescued.
what_went_wrong: The terminal agent (IP) let go of the pilot ladder while descending.
corrective_actions:
• Reduce exposure by restricting pilot ladder personnel transfer to tasks which require physical presence onboard export tanker. Review justification and investigate remote alternative solutions as far as possible.
• Personnel boarding a ship should be in good physical condition and feel confident for climbing the pilot ladder and stepping on the accommodation ladder.
• Where possible, consider a health check by medical personnel for personnel boarding vessels.
• Develop and complete training for the pilot and crew of the crew boat on checking that the pilot ladder and the accommodation ladder is arranged correctly.
• The vessel should make a lee to facilitate boarding. The vessel should be stopped without making way, or sail at a heading and speed agreed between the vessel Master and the pilot of the crew boat to make a good lee.
• Use STOP card when conditions are unsafe or if any defect in boarding arrangements is reported and not corrected.

what_went_wrong:

• Work party supervisor failed to enforce operations exclusion zone.
corrective_actions:

narrative: A beam pump polished rod parted during normal operations. The failure of the polished rod caused three objects, parted polished rod section (19.4kg), rod rotator (18.1kg), and load cell (3.5kg) to be released and fall to the ground, adjacent to the wellhead.
what_went_wrong:
• The shaft had failed due to tensile-tensile or unidirectional bending fatigue failure in the condition of high stress with high stress concentration.
• Bainitic microstructures were evident throughout the thickness of the rod, indicating possible inadequate heat treatment.
• Significant banding was found in the core regions of the rod.
• A significant difference was found between the current results and the hardness data provided in the heat certificate.
• The hardness results shown in the heat certificate were also inconsistent with the expected ultimate tensile strength of the steel.
• The impact strength of the steel was very low for a grade 4140 steel.
corrective_actions:
• Undertake an As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) evaluation to determine if existing controls are sufficient. Identify if additional controls are required to be at ALARP.
• Risk Management: ensure additional controls (drop zones/2-minute time limit) are effectively communicated and applied.
• Inspection/audit: verify that controls are known, implemented, and effective in the field.
• Independent review/inspection by a third-party inspection (failure analysis).
• Organizational failure to adequately learn: similar incidents have occurred within the business, however, after a review of the incidents and associated actions it was identified that they were only partially effective, not fully implemented, and/or not known.

narrative: Operation was in the process of run completion (tubing 2-7/8") to 1164 mAH of 2004 mAH. While the driller lowered the traveling block holding the 2-7/8" tubing, the IP was working in the rig floor area, attempting to hold the tubing with his hand. IP was carrying the tubing, and attempting to hold the tubing for removing the thread protector. The unexpected movement of tubing caused the IP to fall from the rig floor to the catwalk. The rig floor was 3.6 metres from ground level. The catwalk was 0.8 metres from ground level. The IP fell 2.8 metres.
what_went_wrong: From the incident simulation, the YT elevator handle caused the bending of tubing (stored energy) and then released the energy to the IP, which caused him to fall through the V-Door.
corrective_actions:
• Design: The V-shape stopper used to support and lock the travelling block set during rig down for mobilization caused a potential obstruction. YT elevator is normally used due to the more robust locking mechanism. However, the handle of the YT elevator stuck out, creating a risk of obstruction by the V-shaped stopper. Due to operation, the safety chain needs to be removed for the purpose of tubing pick-up activity. Verify the impact of the V-shaped stopper on the mast structure. Remove the V-shaped stopper. A simulation should be run to see if the risk of obstruction has been reduced. Issue a Management of Change (MOC) for the redesign of the latching point for traveling block mobilization. Consider to study the appropriate elevator which is suitable for the flushby unit working condition. Consider alternative fall prevention, e.g., a sliding door or something designed to minimize the opening gap and ensure no one can fall from height and issue an MOC for modification.
• Procedure and safe work practice: The current practice is to handle pipes by hand. Rope or other means for pipe handling would minimize the risk of line of fire and hand on load hazard. Share practice and review work instructions among units under Well Services.
• Human factor: Time out for safety was not effectively implemented to verify the abnormality causing more vibration. No one on the rig floor stopped IP from performing the rig floorman task. Communicate the importance of stop work authority (SWA) and taking time out for safety to all operations.
• Supervision: Toolpusher/Driller did not assign roustabout to replace floorman, causing an unauthorized person to perform a task. There is no clear role and responsibility for interfacing the scope between the rig floor and the completion team. Set up ground rules for manpower arrangements during break time and communicate to all crews. Communicate role and responsibility to all completion and workover crews.

narrative: De-ballast pump was found not electrically isolated, following removal and reinstatement of suction/discharge spooling for flange face inspections. The connecting rod from the isolator handle to the isolation switch was not fully engaged. During the preceding 13 days, flange face inspections/repairs continued, with seven different permit holders, without any further verification of the isolation that was in place. When the Isolating Authority applied the isolation and turned the isolation handle to the 'locked open' position, as per the approved isolation scheme, the internal connecting rod was not fully engaged and consequently slipped, leaving the isolation switch in the 'closed' position. Isolation was independently verified as per requirements, which included cross-checking of the electrical isolation certificate with the appropriate equipment. Verification does not involve, nor require, proving isolation integrity.
what_went_wrong:
• Isolation was ineffective for the equipment, as the isolation handle did not engage fully with the connecting rod and subsequently the isolator switch.
• The isolation standard and associated manuals and procedures are not stringent enough in enforcing the requirements for 'Proving an Isolation'.
corrective_actions:
• Clearly define requirements in the isolation manual around proving isolation integrity and provide examples, including the requirement to 'try test' before starting work. This should take place with the work party and the area authority on initial (first issuance) permit sign-on. This also demonstrates to the work party that the equipment is unavailable and provides an added layer of assurance.
• Effective immediately, during the normal isolation process for LV isolators with connecting rods, prior to the application of lock and tags, open motor control centre module and confirm connecting rod has operated correctly with isolator in the 'OPEN' (Isolated) state. This will also provide another level of assurance for that particular isolation, as the isolator switch/device can be visually inspected to confirm it is in the 'OPEN' (isolated) state.
• Investigate options for potential modifications to the interconnecting rod and handle latch mechanism to increase mechanism reliability.
