narrative: On 22 October 2025 at approximately 1615 hours, smoke alarm detectors were triggered in the engine room. Personnel on Board (POB) mustering and engine room reported one missing person. Emergency Response Team (ERT) deployed to the location and found one engine room operator unconscious, adjacent to steam plant. Additionally, there was sign of steam release found at site. Despite prompt medical attention by the onboard medical team, the individual was subsequently pronounced deceased. The affected equipment and piping were isolated.
what_went_wrong:
This incident was due to the following factors:
a. Condensation-induced water hammer
b. The failure of the end plate weldment
c. The end plate was ejected and hit the DP on the right side of his head
corrective_actions: Gaps in system operation, monitoring, and competency management. This serves as an important reminder of the need for strong technical control and workforce awareness when operating steam systems. This incident highlights the importance of ensuring all crew, especially new and existing personnel, are properly trained and aware of steam system risks such as steam hammering, and are competent in following approved operating procedures. Critical equipment including control valves, steam traps, and piping must be maintained in proper working condition and operated in automatic mode where required to prevent condensate build-up and system damage. Adequate temperature and pressure monitoring must be in place and closely observed so that early intervention can be taken during abnormal conditions. Operating procedures must be regularly reviewed and updated to include steam hammering mitigation measures, and the Management of Change (MoC) process must be strengthened to ensure that any system modifications are properly assessed, documented, and reflected in as-built drawings.

narrative: After replacing the submersible pump of the water pit, it was reported that there was no water flow. The Labour Foreman (LFM) and one Roustabout (deceased) went to check the pump. what_went_wrong:
There were no specifications nor guidance for water pit construction and operations. This includes pump maintenance and accessibility requirements with the associated risk of working near water. Moreover, the construction of the water pit was not included in the location preparation contract.
• No warning signs/barriers provided to prevent entry to water pit and buddy system was not followed in absence of Labour Foreman.
• The Permit to Work raised was under General Lifting Permit and did not cover the water pump replacement. Hence, the risk associated with the pump replacement and the controls are not established.
corrective_actions:

narrative: During repair works on the Oil-Water Emulsion Heater at a Group Station, a fragment of a concrete block fell on a maintenance mechanic. The worker sustained severe physical injuries and passed away in the ambulance during transit to the hospital.
what_went_wrong:
1. Unsafe Acts and Human Factors: Personnel applied an unauthorized "choke hitch" slinging method after the burner became stuck during the initial lifting attempt. The injured worker violated safety protocols by pulling himself up on the burner itself to secure the sling, using the equipment as a physical support. When technical difficulties arose (equipment jamming), the crew failed to stop work for a reassessment of risks, leading to the burner falling along with the worker.
2. Failures in Operational Control: The responsible line supervisor was absent from the high-risk work site, having left for another facility to perform a different task. Oversight regarding the adherence to safety requirements by responsible persons and the employer was deemed insufficient. Despite the existence of a permit-to-work, no actual risk assessment (dynamic risk assessment) was conducted directly at the work site prior to the task.
3. Organizational and Systemic Deficiencies: The technological regulations lacked step-by-step instructions for the dismantling and installation of the burner, leading to dangerous improvisation on-site. Insufficient training and qualification of workers for this specific type of hazardous work were identified. The internal control system failed to provide adequate supervision during the planning and resource allocation stages.
4. Technical Consequences: As a result of falling from height along with the burner, the worker sustained severe injuries. The worker passed away in the ambulance enroute to the hospital.
corrective_actions:
1. Operational Oversight and Supervision: High-risk activities must never be conducted without the continuous presence and active supervision of a designated line supervisor. Supervisors must prioritize safety oversight over secondary tasks; leaving a high-risk site unattended creates a critical vulnerability.
2. Risk Assessment and "Stop Work Authority": A formal risk assessment must be documented and registered before starting any maintenance or dismantling work. Personnel must be empowered and trained to exercise "Stop Work Authority" the moment a task deviates from the plan (e.g., equipment jamming) to perform a dynamic risk reassessment. No work should commence or continue if safety measures are not fully organized or if the situation changes unexpectedly.
3. Technical Documentation and Procedures: Technological regulations must include detailed, step-by-step instructions for specific hazardous tasks, such as burner dismantling, including approved slinging points and methods. All technical procedures should be reviewed to ensure they cover the full lifecycle of the task: setup, execution, and emergency contingencies
4. Competence and Training: Training programs must go beyond general safety and focus on specific, high-risk operational tasks to ensure workers are fully prepared for the technical challenges they may face. Regular safety briefings should reinforce the dangers of using equipment (like burners or piping) as physical supports or climbing aids.
5. Permit-to-Work (PTW) System: The PTW system must be strictly enforced and potentially digitized to ensure all safety barriers are verified and documented by responsible parties before work begins.

narrative: On July 10, 2025, at approximately 7:40 AM, while traveling along public road, a contractor minibus carrying four passengers and a driver was involved in a frontal collision with a third-party truck, which had a single occupant. A third vehicle, a car carrying three passengers, was also involved in the incident. As a result of the collision, one passenger from the minibus and the driver of the truck tragically lost their lives. The remaining minibus occupants sustained injuries of varying severity and were transported to hospital for treatment. The three passengers from the car were medically evaluated and later discharged. Emergency services and another contractor vehicle arrived within minutes, and emergency calls were made.
what_went_wrong: Preliminary indications suggest the car, traveling ahead of the minibus, may have crossed lanes and interacted with the truck, triggering a chain reaction that caused the truck to veer into the minibus's path. The crash occurred rapidly, leaving little time for evasive action. Two passengers who were not wearing seatbelts were ejected from the minibus upon impact. One passenger sustained fatal injuries, while the other was severely injured.
corrective_actions:
1. While Contractor HSSE Management processes are in place and HSSE risks are generally identified as high, inconsistent specification, documentation, and assurance of transport and driver safety requirements - particularly for personnel transportation - can lead to gaps in effective risk mitigation. Clear, consistent contract requirements, robust contractor and subcontractor transport safety capability assessments, aligned HSSE Plans, and disciplined assurance with tracked actions to closure are essential to ensure driver safety risks are adequately managed throughout the contract lifecycle.
2. Transport and driver safety risks were inconsistently identified, embedded, or assured within contractor scopes -particularly in multi-mode contracts - leading to gaps in critical controls such as seatbelt use, fatigue management, and safety technology deployment. Clear scope ownership and active contract holder engagement, as seen in road-transport-focused contracts, are essential to ensure consistent enforcement of legal requirements, driver readiness, and effective use of technology-enabled controls across all transport activities.

narrative: At around 4am on 1st of May, the two men on the crane were assigned to a new location. The operation involved depositing the counterweights. narrative: On 18 August 2025, a team was installing a 6-inch pipe over a 35-metre section between two lines. This pipe was also to be used during WO operations. During the operation, the team separated a 6-inch pipe from a 2-inch pipe, both of which had previously been tied together with cords. During the lifting phase, the cords were gradually cut to separate the two pipes. When the third cord was cut, the tension accumulated in the 6-inch pipe, which was bent at the time, was suddenly released. The pipe rebounded and struck an operator's right leg between the ankle and knee, causing an open fracture. The supervisor was immediately informed, the control room was alerted, and emergency procedures were quickly implemented.
what_went_wrong: PI: Right leg open fracture of staff during the connection operation, while lifting a 6-inch pipe and a 2-inch pipe, both of which had previously been tied together with ropes on the 18th August 2025.
corrective_actions: All work performed requires a dedicated method statement/JHA. The JHA and PTW are updated for all job applicants. Improve the behaviour of the authorities responsible for stopping work at all subcontractors. Review the management of the contract.

narrative: On January 19, 2025, during restart attempts of the HP-A Gas Compressor following corrective maintenance, an unusually loud noise was heard from the exhaust. Seconds later, the fire alarm was triggered, and it was observed that the exhaust structure had fallen off. Technicians in the vicinity immediately pressed the compressor's emergency stop button and evacuated the facility. Simultaneously, the emergency response team was activated, and the on-scene commander initiated a full facility shutdown using a manual call point near the compressor building. Once the source of the loud noise was confirmed to be the HP-A compressor, with the exhaust lying on the ground, the area was cordoned off, and an investigation was launched. The compressor was manually shut down, and the ESD-1 emergency stop was activated.
what_went_wrong: During the starting of gas lift compressor (HP-A), the exhaust pipe of the engine driving the reciprocating compressor broke and fell off after several attempts to start it, subsequently activating the fire alarm.
corrective_actions: The crew was not very familiar with the model of engine and didn't know how to react after 1 or 2 attempts to restart. The operating manual was in English not fully understood by the maintenance team.

narrative: During a heavy rainstorm, two aluminium composite panels (component of the external cladding material for the Office building) dislodged and dropped. The two (2) panels, each weighing 9.8kgs and measuring 1.11x1.49ms, dropped from about a height of 22.35 meters. The fallen panels were found Infront of the South Wing Power room, and the affected area was promptly cordoned off to prevent further hazards. Additionally, multiple panels were observed hanging loosely, posing a potential safety risk to occupants and visitors.
what_went_wrong:
1. Aluminium composite panels not airtight. - Previous investigations revealed that no consideration was given to the potential for panels falling during design and installation. Furthermore, subsequent structural integrity assessments did not clearly establish the mode of failure and effective mitigation measures to prevent recurrence. Additionally, in cases where potentially falling aluminium composite panels have been reported, remedial actions to remove and reinstall such panels are not promptly executed, despite the high potential impact of a dropped panel.
2. Corrective action process not effectively implemented. - There has been recurring near misses involving dropped Aluminium Composite Panels in 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2024. However, corrective actions, such as implementing monthly and quarterly drop inspections, have not been sustained. Furthermore, planned preventive maintenance and other assurance activities that were instituted have not been consistently followed and remain areas requiring improvement. For instance, the annual integrity assessment for 2023 and 2024 were not conducted as planned.
corrective_actions:
1. Conduct an integrity inspection and assessment of the external of the entire building to identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential recurrence of the incident in the short term.
2. Re-institute the conduct of the annual inspection programme of the entire exterior of the building's facade to identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential dropped objects.

narrative: At about 02:21hrs, while rig crew was picking 4" drill pipe, a single drill pipe was picked from Catwalk to the rig floor with Air winch tugger. The IP removed thread protector from the single pipe while another floorman attempted to guide the pipe into the mouse hole. The pipe missed the mouse hole, hit the rig floor and also hit the IP on his right ear and shoulder. IP was move to Clinic.
what_went_wrong:
1. Lowering without signal - The air tugger operator lowered the pipe without receiving a stop/lower command, due to absence of a dedicated signaller and reliance on previous experience racking 11 stands without one.
2. Obstructed line of sight - The operator was blindsided by the position of already-racked pipes, limiting visibility of the mousehole area.
3. IP in fall zone - The injured person was inadvertently in the trajectory of the falling pipe after removing the thread protector.
4. Incoherent communication - The floormen recognized the pipe had missed the mousehole but were only able to shout warnings, which were not effectively received
corrective_actions:
1. Updating and endorsing the racking SOP.
2. Assigning a dedicated signaller for all pipe-handling operations.
3. Adjusting derrick camera positioning to restore clear line of sight.
4. Reinforcing communication protocols and hazard-zone controls.

narrative: On 3rd June 2025, at about 2:15pm, during a test digging on a 6" test line right of way, the excavator bucket made contact with a buried 11KVA composite electrical cable. The incident resulted in a dent/superficial cut on the cable.
what_went_wrong:
1. The excavator was used to accelerate exposure of an underground pipeline despite the presence of multiple buried utilities.
2. The as-built survey lacked sufficient detail, particularly regarding test line depth and exact routing, leading to misinterpretation of subsurface conditions.
3. During test digging, the excavator bucket contacted a buried 11 kVA composite electrical cable, causing a dent and minor cut.
4. Excavator use in close proximity to unidentified/poorly defined underground assets introduced a line-strike hazard.
corrective_actions:
1. Mechanical excavation (excavators) must not be used near unknown or insufficiently verified buried utilities.
2. Probing results identifying multiple underground facilities must trigger manual excavation only.
3. As-built drawings must be accurate, up-to-date, and detailed, especially regarding depth and horizontal spacing.
4. When indications are unclear, stop work and escalate for engineering verification.

narrative: A 9 kg metal plate detached from the conveyor railway and fell approximately 6.5-10 m onto the deck below. No personnel were struck; however, dropped-object energy indicated fatality potential. The plate was originally installed as a dropped-object prevention measure. Over time it deteriorated and was displaced due to a misaligned and stretched conveyor belt, which pushed the plate out of position. Operations on the starboard conveyor were stopped, the area below was barricaded, and a rope-access inspection of similar installations was initiated.
what_went_wrong:
• Dropped-object protection plate was not adequately inspected or maintained over time.
• Conveyor belt was poorly fitted/misaligned, creating continuous mechanical load on the plate.
• No inspection programme identified deterioration or displacement risk.Safety-critical equipment (secondary retention / guarding) was not recognised as such and therefore not verified.
• Asset integrity management and preventative maintenance were ineffective.
corrective_actions:
• Treat dropped-object prevention devices (guards, covers, retention plates) as safety-critical equipment requiring routine inspection.
• Implement a formal inspection and maintenance programme for conveyors and associated guards.
• Correct belt alignment and tension to prevent abnormal loads on structures.
• Periodically survey elevated plant for dropped-object hazards (e.g., DROPS inspections/rope access).
• Ensure barricading/red-zone control beneath overhead equipment during operations where deterioration is possible.

narrative: At approximately 06:30, lifting operations were being conducted to move spools from the main deck to the cellar/sub-cellar deck. Because no direct lifting path existed, the crew chose to lift the load through a slickline hatch, which constituted a complex lift and was not covered by the approved PTW. The crane operator had no line of sight and was communicating by radio only. During lifting, the hook snagged the hatch plate. The rigger, who was standing on the hatch cover to guide the load, attempted to stop the lift. The plate dislodged and the rigger fell approximately 6.5 m to the deck below. The injured person was medevaced with serious injuries. The event had clear fatality potential.
what_went_wrong:
• A complex lifting operation was performed under a PTW that only authorised a standard lift.
• Work scope changed without risk assessment or lift planning.
• Crane operator had no line of sight and communications were unreliable.
• Rigger stood on the hatch cover to guide the load, placing himself in a fall hazard zone.
• The lift was coordinated using voice/radio in a noisy area without clear signalling control.
• Rigger's certification had expired and supervision was inadequate.
• Unsafe practice had become normalised due to prior similar lifts performed without incident.
corrective_actions:
• Complex lifts require a specific lift plan, risk assessment, and supervision.
• Never route loads through hatches/openings without engineered lifting arrangements.
• Maintain line of sight or use a designated trained signalman with agreed communication protocol.
• Personnel must never stand on removable covers or under suspended loads.
• Verify competency and certification of riggers and lifting personnel.
• Stop work when lift conditions differ from the approved plan.

narrative: While parking the starboard (STBD) crane following routine lifting operations, the crane boom was brought down into the boom rest abruptly rather than in a controlled manner. narrative: During pallet racking activities in the warehouse, a forklift was in the process of lifting a pallet to the third shelf. what_went_wrong: Incompatibility between the forklift (material handling equipment) in use and the racking system configuration installed. The distance between shelf three and shelf four was 1350mm. The height of the forklift backrest was 1250mm. This left 100mm between the two and when manoeuvring the load into position resulted in the load above being lifted inadvertently. The higher you lift the forklift mast, the more important adequate clearances become.
corrective_actions: Equipment Compatibility Must Be Verified - Ensure all material handling equipment and load types are assessed for compatibility with racking systems before use or when managing change. This includes verifying dimensions and manoeuvrability. Critical Importance of Adequate Clearance - Maintain safe clearance margins between shelving levels, loads and the material handling equipment, especially when operating at height.

The communication method(s) for the use of the Stop Work Authority for all personnel involved in the activity, must be clearly understood and tested prior to activity commencement.

narrative: When filling a mud tank with brine to prepare for cleaning of the tank, the transfer hose became dislodged, fell towards the ground (2.6m) and began to whip. The hose struck the pump operator's leg, who suffered a ruptured Achilles tendon. The operator required surgery, classifying this as a Lost Work Day Case under IOGP guidelines. The incident is considered high potential, as the heavy hose coupling could have caused a fatality if it struck the head of the injured person when it fell.
what_went_wrong: The original configuration of the activity was changed by the work team to run the lay-flat 'fire' hose into the top of the mud tank where there was no connection point. The pump was started without the hose being properly restrained and flow was too strong for the arrangements, causing the hose to dislodge and fall towards the injured person who was operating the pump at the base of the mud tank. Before the change in the configuration of the work, the job had been considered low risk. The change in risk introduced was not realised by the work team, who did not forecast potential movement of the hose.
corrective_actions:
Immediate actions:
1. Immediately issue / communicate a site instruction (or similar) requiring securing of hoses and hose ends
2. As an instruction, or an additional step in the risk assessment for the main tank cleaning job, state a preference to use a vacuum truck for filling, and if not available, acceptable alternative arrangements. Include hose type, suitable pump sizes, hose securing to tank utilizing fixed points, protection against failure of the system (e.g. whip checks) and position of people. Preventative actions:
3. Committed to installing fixed hose connections to all tanks and chambers within the tanks to ensure hoses remain fixed and secure during pumping activities.
4. Implement dynamic risk assessment programme: Personnel will need to be trained on this simple process and when to conduct it (e.g. before each new task, a change, or a change in the mode of work or location). Such a process will provide a 'pause' before work, giving an opportunity to review risks and team actions, even for work that does not require a permit or formal risk assessment.

narrative: On 8 October 2025 on an offshore rig, a lifting operation was underway to land an 11.8 m, 2.67 ton bottom hole assembly (BHA) into a storage basket on the riser deck. During the final positioning, the BHA made a sudden uncontrolled movement. The forward end either contacted the basket edge, rotating the load toward the injured person, or the crane made an unintended movement. The injured person was positioned in a narrow space between riser guide posts with no escape route available. He had earlier climbed onto adjacent baskets and manually guided the load several times to open covers in the inner basket. The BHA struck him in the chest and compressed him against another basket. Emergency response was immediate, and medical evacuation was carried out via search and rescue (SAR) helicopter. what_went_wrong: Hands-free lifting methods were not used despite being available, exposing personnel to the line of fire. The crane was operated by a trainee without required mentor supervision, contrary to procedure. The lift was treated as a routine task, and risk assessment did not account for congested deck layout, lack of escape routes, basket orientation requirements, or blind zones for the crane operator. The BHA was landed the wrong way due to missing communication, partly caused by language barriers. The deck was heavily congested, forcing the injured person into restricted and hazardous positions to open basket covers and guide the BHA manually. No exclusion zone was established. Several crew members were new in roles or on the rig, and norms for intervening or stopping unsafe work were inconsistent. Organisational follow-up on competence, planning quality, and supervision responsibilities was insufficient. These factors created multiple error traps and eliminated critical barriers.
corrective_actions: Lifting operations involving heavy BHA components require detailed planning that reflects actual deck conditions, special equipment requirements, and correct use of hands-free practices. Exclusion zones and escape routes must always be established and maintained. Trainee crane operators must only operate under direct mentor supervision in accordance with formal competence requirements. Communication expectations with third-party vendors must be clear, including language-barrier mitigation. Deck layout planning between logistics and lifting operations must ensure safe accessibility, visibility, and controlled load movement. Stop-work authority must be reinforced culturally to empower all personnel to intervene. Competence verification prior to mobilisation and clearer integration of procedures into workflow are essential to prevent recurrence.

narrative: An operator was removing a grating panel with manual handling hooks on the weather deck. During the operation, the grating unhooked from the manual handling tools and fell through the opening, hit a cable gate before landing on the underlying deck, approximately 10 meters below. The grating measures 1x1 meter and weighs 52,4 kg which gives a kinetic energy of 5149, 44 Joules. No one was injured, but under slightly changed circumstances people could have been in the line of fire as the deck was not cordoned off and there was a work team close to the area where it dropped.
what_went_wrong: The grating was not physically secured. During job preparation, the work crew had not reviewed all the required safety measures before starting the job, nor verified that they had been implemented, such as securing tools and equipment to prevent them from falling and barricading the area below the work site. No supervisor present to correct.
corrective_actions:
• When working at height, it is essential to ensure that tools and equipment are secured to prevent falling objects, in accordance with life-saving rules.
• When installing grating, it must always be secured with a fixed barrier, such as a shackle or wire/sling (the two-barrier principle), as shown in the image to the right.
• Grating like this should be secured to the structure above the work area. The securing equipment should be as short as practically possible.
• The area below must always be sufficiently cordoned off.

narrative: During platform crane lifting operations to land a container on the main deck North landing, the IP sustained a crush/impact injury to shoulder/ribs. The crane and container were made safe and the individual treated by platform advanced first aider followed by coastguard medevac for further assessment.
what_went_wrong:
• No verbal communication from banksman to crane operator of bridle being located in skip or not yet disconnected at time of verbal instruction "Up on your line".
• Banksman did not give clear communications to the crane operator and no use of confirmatory communications / protocols.
• No agreed set terminology or signals for free hook.
• No information passed to crane operator that the hook was in the skip and there were issues with disconnecting it.
• No crane motion instruction should have been issued by the banksman to the crane operator whilst the slinger was in the line of fire position.
• Poor communications led to assumption by crane operator that the hook was free.
• Banksman did not instruct Slinger to move out of Line of Fire prior to instructing Crane Op to go "Up on your line".
corrective_actions: There is no such thing as a routine activity - there are only repeat activities under different conditions that each needs to be understood and risk assessed. Maintain vigilance at all times. Safety Critical verbal communications need to be clear, concise and unambiguous to minimise the risk of incorrect interpretation. In safety critical tasks where there is no visual contact between work party members, confirmatory verbal communication should be used to verify understanding of commands (e.g. blind lifts, applying inhibits). Hazards may be constantly changing in nature throughout an activity. Wherever possible, removing the hazard or work parties' exposure to the hazard should be the priority in risk assessment- in this case "line of fire". narrative: A forklift driver's ankle was struck by a spreader bar during offloading from a truck at the logistics base. There were no lifting pockets welded onto the bar. In past lifting operations, the spreader bar had been placed on wooden blocks on the truck bed and lifted directly on the forks of a forklift. This time the wooden blocks were not in place. The truck driver and the forklift driver decided to lift the spreader bar off the truck by hooking hoisting slings attached to the spreader bar and to the forklift forks, crossing them to reduce the length of the slings. During hoisting, the spreader bar rotated and swung into the forklift cabin, hitting the driver's ankle. The forklift cabin door had been left open to improve communication between the drivers.
what_went_wrong:
1. Uncontrolled movement of the spreader bar due to hoisting the bar with slings hung from the forklift forks.
2. Forklift door left open for verbal communication.
3. Use of incorrect equipment to carry out the lift - it is forbidden to put slings directly onto the forks of a forklift, the spreader bar was not equipped with forklift pockets, a forklift hoisting adaptor was not available, a crane lift should have been utilised.
4. No lifting plan, job instructions or procedures in place, thus no management of change applied.
5. Inadequate induction and training for forklift drivers and visiting truck drivers.
6. Supervisor absent due to long-lasting illness, no official replacement.
7. High turnover of personnel at the logistics base.
corrective_actions:
1. Ensure all lifts performed with Forklift are covered by a procedure or lifting plan.
2. Specify the requirements for lifting operations in site training and induction programmes for the appropriate supply base personnel.
3. Check that the equipment needed to adapt forklifts for the expected loads is in place at site, and Operators are trained to safely use it.

narrative: On an offshore drilling rig, on 1 September 2025, personnel and marine crew were installing handrails on top of a unit on the main deck. Handrail sections (60-90 kg) were lifted by deck crane to the top of the unit, where an operator worked at height to receive and install them, using fall-arrest equipment. The operator initially attached his lanyard to the stairs, then to handrail, and later to another section to reach the final corner section. To fit the last section, he had to lift and adjust some of the handrail. The locking pins were weakly retained and the chain/carabiner secondary securing arrangement did not prevent them from sliding out. The section of the handrail tilted and fell, pulling the operator with it. He fell approximately 4.3 m to deck, landing partly on the fallen handrail. The incident resulted in an LTI and a dropped object with calculated energy of 2733 J, with assessed potential for a single fatality.
what_went_wrong: The units were not designed to support safe work at height: the only structurally adequate anchoring points (lifting eyes) were located below top deck level and were occupied by lifting bridles during installation, leaving no suitable anchor points available. The operator therefore clipped his fall-arrest lanyard to a handrail section that was only temporarily secured by a pin, chain, and carabiner. The handrail securing design was inherently weak; on the short side of the container, the locking pin had only ~2 mm mechanical engagement and could easily slide out, and the chain/carabiner arrangement offered a false sense of security. The installation and commissioning procedure mentioned work at height and scaffolding, but did not clearly explain how the handrails should be installed or secured, nor the purpose or requirement for scaffold. No scaffold was erected, and the crew changed the intended installation sequence, requiring lifting and moving the section used as an anchor. Competence requirements for work at height (Norog 113) were not formalised in the competence matrix; several involved personnel lacked formal practical WAH training and were unaware of approved anchor point requirements. Project planning and follow-up from onshore were insufficient, and the contractor equipment checklist process was not effectively applied.
corrective_actions: Work at height must never rely on temporary structures (such as partially installed handrails) as anchoring points. Units that require routine or installation work at height must be designed with suitable, certified anchor points, or work must be carried out from properly designed scaffolding or other engineered access solutions. Competence requirements for working at height (incl. practical training and anchor-point assessment) must be explicitly built into contractor competence matrices and verified before mobilisation. Installation and commissioning procedures for vendor packages must clearly describe safe installation methods, including detailed handrail installation sequences, locking mechanisms, and when scaffolding is mandatory. Work permits that bundle many high-risk activities can obscure critical controls; large scopes should be broken into smaller work procedures where necessary to ensure hazards and controls are fully understood. A robust equipment and project-follow-up process is needed, including use of the correct contractor equipment checklist and clear assignment of onshore and offshore responsibility for installation planning and oversight.

narrative: In connection with a pigging operation on an offshore installation, several pigs weighing 35 - 40 kg were lowered from a scaffold using rope, as the pig receiver was placed 5m above the turret deck. When the last pig was being lowered, the knot loosened, and the pig fell onto the turret deck and then bounced outside the barrier and down onto the tank deck. The need to lower the pigs from the 5m high scaffold where the pigging took place was not included in planning and risk assessments. Issues of logistics and material handling were given too little consideration, special lifting expertise has not been sufficiently involved.
corrective_actions:
• Planning/risk assessment of operation - include logistic, not just the operation itself and ensure the right competence is included
• Ensure that adequate area is properly cordoned off

narrative: Collision between northern crane and derrick resulting in falling objects.
what_went_wrong: Three objects fell after the north crane collided with the derrick. The crane operator had been planning to perform lubrication of the slewing ring with the logistics discipline responsible for some time, but this was changed to the crane operator bringing along a deck operator who was being trained as a crane-operator. A helicopter was on its way to the platform, and they had about 25 minutes to finish before the helicopter arrived. It was decided that the crane operator was to perform the lubrication in the crane pedestal while the deck operator operated the crane. The crane was lifted and swung out over the sea. The crane operator reminded to "elevate the crane-boom" to avoid the derrick and then went down into the pedestal. The deck operator elevated the boom and swung the crane towards the platform. After a brief stop to change the lubrication cartridge, the crane was topped up a little more before it swung further towards the derrick. The deck operator believed the boom was topped up enough. The walkway and the spotlight mounted on the right side of the boom were driven into the upper corner of the wind wall high up in the derrick. narrative: Two personnel experienced symptoms of severe oxygen deficiency during inspection work, but managed to self-evacuate safely. Subsequent measurements confirmed low oxygen levels inside the enclosure, linked to nitrogen ingress from the turbine seal system combined with a lack of ventilation.
what_went_wrong: The incident was triggered by nitrogen leakage from the seal system, which under normal ventilated conditions is harmless. However, following a planned emergency shutdown (ESD) and blackstart prior to shutdown period, key barriers were unavailable: ventilation remained off, and the fire dampers which require manual reopening, stayed closed. Without airflow, oxygen was gradually displaced overnight creating a hazardous atmosphere that posed a serious risk of unconsciousness and fatality.
corrective_actions: Assess feasibility of installing fixed oxygen monitoring in the turbine enclosure and similar areas. If not feasible, require mandatory portable gas testing before entry into locations with potential oxygen depletion risk. Review and update the blackstart procedure to ensure turbine hood ventilation and dampers are restored before the area is reclassified as safe for entry. Revise PTW requirements for entries into the turbine enclosure during or after special operational states (e.g., blackstart, shutdown, or loss of HVAC). The PTW must account for potential atmospheric changes, with mandatory portable gas measurements under such conditions.

narrative: During preparations for installing a 20'' sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician's hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed.
what_went_wrong: The sealing ring was tested earlier than planned, without expanding the barricaded area and without informing the crew below. The ring slipped due to inadequate handling conditions (gloves, oily surface). The work area had been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed in the elevated area during phase one, creating exposure before barriers were in place. Barricading was too small, based on a common but unsafe practice of using minimal exclusion zones for "non-loose object" work at height. Communication between team members and between teams and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent of barricading but did not verify it physically. The team lead was cognitively overloaded and new in the role, reducing situational awareness. Stop-work authority was not used despite unease among personnel below. The net result was coexistence of workers above and below with no effective barrier against dropped objects.
corrective_actions: All work at height must assume potential for falling objects and require full barricading unless a technical barrier (e.g., safety net) is installed. Equipment must not be brought into elevated areas before controls are in place. Area technicians must physically verify barricades before work starts. Practices that rely on personnel remembering not to bring loose items into height work are insufficient; technical and organizational barriers must supplement human behaviour. SIMOPS coordination must be strengthened, including explicit identification of all nearby work teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally within teams must be improved to ensure shared situational awareness. Stop-work authority must be normalised, supported, and used proactively. Project-wide learning should be shared across platforms to eliminate similar practices elsewhere.

narrative: During the night shift, the crew attempted to release an anchor latch tool from a permanent packer using a straight pull of 60 klbs (including 55 klbs string weight) without success. Following contractors' procedures, the string was tensioned with 5 klbs over string weight and rotated manually, but no movement was observed. Based on contractors' instructions, power tongs were partially used due to the absence of a power swivel on site. During the sixth right-hand turn with a 5 klbs overpull, the 2-7/8" tubing coupling connected to the safety valve backed off and fell approximately 21 ft onto the rig floor, then a further 14 ft to the ground. At the same time, the tubing string settled approximately 6 ft into the packer. The combined weight of the coupling and safety valve was 36.5 kg.
what_went_wrong:
1. Uncontrolled rotation using a power tong led to the tubing connection backing off.
2. Thread make-up integrity was not sufficient for rotation under tension.
3. Lack of appropriate equipment (power swivel) resulted in the use of a higher-risk alternative.
4. Dropped-object controls were inadequate, allowing heavy equipment to fall from height.
corrective_actions:
1. Management of Change (MoC) must be applied before deviation. Any deviation from approved procedures, tooling, or operating limits shall be formally reviewed, risk-assessed, and approved through the MBPS MoC process prior to execution.
2. Operations must stop when normal operating parameters are exceeded. When loads, methods, or equipment differ from the original plan, supervisors must stop work and reassess using approved Operator procedures and MoC requirements.
3. Contractually required equipment must be available and used as intended. Operations shall not proceed unless all contract-specified rig equipment is present, functional, and fit for purpose. Temporary or partial substitutions are not acceptable.
4. Stop Work Authority (SWA) must be actively exercised and enforced. All personnel are required to stop work when unsafe conditions exist, including dropped-object exposure, lack of secondary retention, or use of non-approved tools or methods.
5. Secondary retention is mandatory for elevated components. All elevated or moving tools and components shall be secured with secondary retention wherever practicable to prevent dropped-object incidents.
6. Roles and scopes of work must be clearly understood and respected. Operators and service providers shall operate strictly within their defined scopes of work, with no overreach beyond assigned responsibilities.

narrative: A contractor mechanical field service representative and mechanical team had disconnected the export gas compressor gas turbine's primary and secondary flexible fuel gas hoses. After disconnecting the hoses, the contractor field service representative was on the back side of the gas turbine while the mechanical technicians were on the front side. While lying beneath the gas turbine to check the water wash drain tube under the gas turbine, pressure was released, causing the loose hoses to swing.
what_went_wrong: One of the loose hoses struck the helmet of the mechanical field service representative, resulting in physical damage to the helmet.
corrective_actions:
• Trapped pressure must always be safely discharged before disconnecting components, even when the system appears isolated - especially in high-pressure gas systems.
• Contractor activities must be fully integrated into company isolation procedures, including proper documentation in Process Isolation Certificates, to avoid oversight of critical steps.
• Safe Work Method Statements (SWMS) must include detailed, step-by-step instructions, particularly for non-routine tasks, to ensure consistent understanding and execution.
• Non-routine activities require Task Risk Assessments (TRA) regardless of pressure levels or perceived risk, as they often involve unexpected hazards.
• System manipulations (e.g., Programmable Logic Controller forcing) must not occur without coordination and approval from the Area Authority, and only after confirming all personnel are in safe positions.

corrective_actions:

• Ensure that a quality inspection for weld hinges is conducted on all gates.
• Ensure that regular inspection and maintenance, including lubrication, are conducted for all gates.
• The operational manual for gates shall be provided and included into the Job Safety Analysis (JSA).
• All gates to be operated within the design limits by trained personnel to prevent damage of gates/hinges.
• Ensure that gates to blasting and painting bays are open during heavy winds to allow for unobstructed airflow.
• During windy conditions, all movable objects/equipment/tools should be properly secured/stored

narrative: A trailer driver was transporting six concrete barriers (3.5t each) on a flatbed trailer. The barriers were stacked in two rows (three in each row), with one cargo lashing belt securing two concrete barriers each. While the trailer was travelling on the bumpy road, the driver noticed that one of the lashing belts securing the rear concrete barriers had broken, causing the load to shift slightly towards the edge of the trailer. He pulled over to address the situation. Fortunately, no injuries or damage occurred.
what_went_wrong:
• The concrete barriers were loaded onto the truck without appropriate measures in place - no dunnage was used and there was inadequate load restraint.
• The driver used improvised lashing belts without proper inspection. One of these improvised belts broke during transportation on the bumpy road.
• The driver did not recognise the risk of using defective and improvised lashing belts.
corrective_actions:
• Always ensure all loads are properly loaded and restrained in accordance with appropriate lashing protocols to prevent them from shifting during transportation.
• Always use additional support systems like rubber mats and/or dunnage to increase the clamp down effect (friction between the load and the trailer surface) to prevent the load from shifting.
• Always ensure loading crews and driver clearly understand the importance of the pre-trip Inspection - lashing belts and tools must be thoroughly inspected for wear, damage, and suitability before departure. Early detection of weakened or compromised equipment can prevent incidents.
• Always ensure corrective actions are implemented at the earliest opportunity to prevent recurrence of similar incidents/accidents - there was a similar incident three months earlier.

narrative: A telehandler operator was moving a 714kg pipe spool when he observed a trailer blocking his access. The operator pulled the telehandler over to the side waiting for the trailer to move away. When the trailer moved, the operator started to reverse the telehandler. After reversing approximately 2 metres, the front right tyre of the telehandler failed and exploded. The release of pressure ejected the tyre 7 metres away from the telehandler. The primary locking rim (weight 19.3kg) and the secondary locking rim (weight 2.3kg) were ejected from the split rim, causing the primary locking rim to land 50 metres away and the secondary locking rim to land 70 metres away. No injuries were reported. The Flagman and Rigger were positioned behind the telehandler approximately 5 metres away.
what_went_wrong:
• Incorrect installation and assembly of tyre/wheel rim.
• During manoeuvring, the load could have potentially shifted to the right side of the forks due to incorrect securing of the pipe spool.
• Over-pressure within the tyre (pinch resulting in the failure of the tyre innertube).
• The daily telehandler checklist does not include tyre condition or tyre pressure. Three tyres were found to be new, and one tyre was damaged.
corrective_actions:
• Equipment operators should be provided with tyre pressure gauges to ensure adequate tyre pressure.
• Improvement of daily checklists with option of multiple languages and requirement of checking tyre pressures.
• On-the-Job Training (OJT) on tyre pressures/condition and the use of gauges to be provided to all equipment operators.
• OJT training video to be prepared to demonstrate the correct installation method of tyre and rims. To be shown to all Plant Maintenance & Vehicle (PMV) team members who are assigned the task of changing tyres.
• All subcontractors PMV groups to identify and physically check all vehicles and equipment on the project that are fitted with split rim wheels. Any vehicle that is identified as having incorrectly fitted spilt rims or misaligned parts should be taken out of service until rectified.

narrative: An 800-ton crawler crane and a 280-ton crawler crane had concluded lifting operations and were idle. A civil crew requested the 800-ton crane operator to reposition the hook so they could avoid working under it. While slewing, the boom tip section of the 800-ton crawler crane contacted the wire rope of the stationary 280-ton crawler crane. The crane was operating within a barricaded area. No visible damage was found on both crawler cranes, and there were no injuries
what_went_wrong:
• The 800-ton crane operator slewed the crane without the presence of the rigging crew or Signalman.
• The 800-ton crane operator failed to identify the obstruction on the slewing path (the 280-ton crane boom positioned over the pipe rack).
• Failure to develop and implement a formal process or procedure to manage simultaneous crane operations.
• Lack of communication - the 280-ton crane was mobilised with its luffing boom extended approximately 6 metres over the pipe rack into the 800-ton crane's work area, without coordination.
corrective_actions:
• Always maintain proper coordination with nearby lifting groups when operating cranes near other activities.
• Never slew or reposition a crane without a Signalman's assistance.
• Implement a formal Simultaneous Operations (SIMOPS) procedure to safely manage multi-crane operations.
• Conduct a pre-lift LMRA to identify potential obstructions in the crane's path.
• Ensure clear and effective communication between crane operators, rigging crews, and other involved teams.

narrative: Power cable damage during excavation.
what_went_wrong: The incident resulted from inadequate excavation planning, including missing cable markers, an overly shallow trial pit that failed to expose the deeper 11 kV cable, the absence of cable detection tools, and the use of mechanical excavation where manual digging was required. These issues were compounded by missing underground service drawings and a Permit to Work issued without proper site inspection.
corrective_actions:
• Always use cable detection tools (e.g., cable locators) before starting any excavation work.
• Always review the appropriate area drawings prior to beginning excavation activities.
• Excavation certificates must only be approved after verifying all cable routes.
• The issuing authority must conduct a detailed site inspection before approving a Permit to Work.
• Define and enforce minimum trial pit depth requirements based on cable burial standards to ensure accurate detection prior to excavation.

narrative: On 30/04/2025, a High Potential (HIPO) occurred when a crane's counterweight of 15 tonnes fell off the trailer due to failure in the securing belt. The trailer was moving from the laydown area to the well-pad. No personnel injuries were reported.
what_went_wrong:
• The trailer was hired from supplier/vendor for material transportation and driver was not aware of the road condition and associated hazards.
• The lashing chain hooks slipped from the secure position and became loose due to vibration while driving on rough road.
• Land transport risk assessment was not updated and discussed with drivers using rough grade access roads.
• Pads or wooden frame were not provided under the load to avoid slippage from the metal surface of trailer bed.
• No escort was provided with heavy transportation to guide the trailer driver.
• All required inspection, documents relevant to the low bed trailer and driver was updated and approved by the project.
corrective_actions:
• Drivers should be educated for unseen uneven road conditions prior to start traveling.
• Risk Assessment shall be revisited and additional lashing prior to transportation on rough roads shall be added as controls.

narrative: After completing the second gyro survey, the crew began rigging down. On the platform deck, a tugger line was attached to the gyro tool as secondary retention. The tool was lifted to the rig floor using the wireline. Once above the rotary table, the wireline gooseneck was installed on top of the tool. The gooseneck, weighing 2.3 kg, fell approximately 50 ft from the rotary table to the platform deck.
what_went_wrong:
• The securing bolt on the gooseneck was damaged during a previous run and replaced. However, the replacement bolt lacked the attachment for the secondary gooseneck retention device. As a result, the operation was carried out without the required safety retention device installed.

corrective_actions:

• Secondary retention devices are safety-critical controls and shall not be removed, bypassed, or omitted without formal engineering justification and authorization.
• Critical procedural requirements must be complied with at all times, without exception, including during routine, non-routine, and close-out activities.
• Always follow red zone management, no simultaneous activities during rig-down.

narrative: The rig crew were in the process of nipple down the bell nipple mandrel. While positioning the multi purpose crane for installing the bell nipple lifting slings the man basket (354kg), which was holding 2 persons, dislodged from the main structure of the crane and fell approx.16.5m to the top deck of the platform. Neither of the 2 persons fell as they were suspended by their harness and inertia reels. Both personnel were recovered in 2 minutes. One of the 2 personnel received first aid treatment for slight swelling.
what_went_wrong:
1. Rotation of man basket around crane winch drum collar created momentum:
a) System has always been "sticky" with the man basket not self-levelling.
b) Rig crew have developed processes to correct (jumping and operate the winch slightly) that are not included in the procedures.
2. Crane wire fitted with shackle caught on man basket structure resulted in lift forces.
3. Combination of forces resulted in man basket lifting and twisting away from the sheave.
4. Multipurpose Crane not being operated as per OEM requirements when DMB installed:
a) Man-basket should not move independently of the crane sheave.
b) Moving the controls to the man basket is a requirement within the manual. This releases the drive motor from the sheave and allows the sheave to rotate freely.
5. Man-basket safety device deployed but not effective:
a) Deemed ineffective following a past incident at another location.
b) OEM's recommendations regarding the new design and the additional inspections were not considered.
corrective_actions:
1. Reinforce the importance of using independent fall arrest equipment when working at height
2. Reinforce the requirement carefully considering attachment points for fall arrest equipment.
3. Ensure that fall arrest equipment is inspected and certified as per Company Procedure.
4. Reinforce the importance of maintaining, storing and inspecting all safety critical equipment to ensure it is in excellent working order when being used.

narrative: During the workboat transfer operation, workboat was transferred from the laydown area to the transport vessel main deck and positioned in its transport cradle. During final positioning, the vessel could not remain steady. As a result, the workboat swung into a nearby Cargo Carrying Unit (CCU), causing damage to the hull. A crew member handling a tag line was exposed to risk and was nearly caught between the CCU and the swinging workboat.
what_went_wrong:
• Clear Deck policy (no persons on deck during lifting operations) not adhered.
• Use of tag lines should have been properly assessed and if required, deviated against.
• Permit to work not used as per vessel Bridging document, for control of non routine tasks within safety zone.
• Methodology for transferring the workboat was not adequality assessed (MoC) rather a generic lifting risk assessment was used.
• Banksman did not have direct communication with vessel bridge, who were responsible for vessel positioning.
• Escape route for those involved in lifting route not clear, potential crushing scenario against container on deck, as work boat swung once lifted out of cradle.
corrective_actions:
• Provide an approved and certified cradle for workboats intended for lifting operations.
• Issue and reinforce a mandatory safety communication during safety meetings emphasizing the requirement for personnel involved in lifting operations to maintain a clear and unobstructed escape route.
• Review the competency levels of personnel involved in lifting operations and provide retraining where gaps are identified.
• Issue a formal communication requiring permit-to-work compliance and task-specific risk assessments for all non-routine activities within designated safety zones.
• Amend the company standard to formally include the prohibition of tag lines and the requirement to maintain a clear deck policy during boat lifting operations.

narrative: On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was released from hospital the same day.
what_went_wrong: The 10" gate valve used as a single isolation was not fully closed because the chain operator seized due to physical interference, giving a false indication that the valve was seated. Pressure verification showed 0 kPag, but this was ambiguous because the flare system was under slight vacuum, meaning zero pressure did not confirm positive isolation. Oxygen entered the flare piping system through the partially open valve while the flare remained lit, creating conditions for ignition. When work was performed on the spectacle blind, this led to a deflagration and an uncontrolled release of energy that injured the worker.
corrective_actions:
1. Zero pressure does not equal positive isolation - Pressure indication alone is an insufficient barrier for verifying isolation in flare systems, especially where vacuum conditions can exist.
2. Single isolation is not a robust barrier for breaking containment - Single isolation provides little tolerance for hidden failures and should not be relied upon where severe energy release is credible.
3. Equipment condition and work environment directly shape human decision-making - People act on the cues the system gives them; degraded equipment and obstructed layouts can actively mislead competent workers.
4. Permits and risk classification must reflect real hazard potential - Administrative controls lose credibility when they do not reflect the true severity of the hazard.

narrative: During a fluid-hauling task, water transfer to a tank truck was completed and the hose was disconnected. A valve was found not fully closed, and hot fluid sprayed during subsequent valve manipulation. The job was stopped, emergency medical response was initiated, and the well/site was shut down to support response and control the release.
what_went_wrong: Residual energy remained in the system at the time of disconnection/valve manipulation, resulting in a hot-fluid spray. The investigation identified gaps in procedural requirements for verifying zero energy and specifying chemical PPE for hot-fluid tasks, and noted that the system configuration did not readily allow field verification of "zero energy."
corrective_actions: Update procedures and minimum PPE requirements for hot-fluid tasks (including defined thresholds) and incorporate explicit "verify zero energy" expectations. Where verification is not practicable, implement engineering/administrative improvements (e.g., bleed/verification points or safer valve/coupler configurations) so that residual energy can be confirmed and controlled before disconnecting equipment.

what_went_wrong: The load became unstable during the unstrapping step and a beam dropped unexpectedly. corrective_actions: Require that all personnel involved in delivery/offloading are included in the pre-job briefing and the offload plan. narrative: A Mechanic and an E-Tech were repairing a section of the natural gas manifold on frac pump. The employees were replacing a section on the manifold referred to as a pistol. After the repairs were made the employees opened the natural gas supply valve to supply the gas manifold on the pump. The mechanic stepped up onto a platform to open the main ball valve of the natural gas manifold to allow the pump to start burning the natural gas as fuel. As the mechanic (IP) opened the main ball valve, both employees heard a loud pop noise. The top of the low-pressure regulator (VDR) broke away from its base and struck the mechanic in the head above his right eye causing a laceration. The top of the VDR is made of aluminum and weighs approximately 1lb/~454g. The IP was evaluated at a local emergency room, and the IP received 8 sutures to close the laceration.
what_went_wrong:
• No administrative controls to perform LOTO on the pump for this task.
• Worker was new to position (little over 3 months) and never worked on gas train.
• Safeguard was not in place and caused the system to be over pressured at 115psi. The OEM rating is 5 psi.
corrective_actions:
• All pumps without complete gas trains were placed out of service and the lock out tag out procedure put into place.
• Training was given to shop & test stand employees on the recognition of a complete gas train and procedure for testing regulators before leaving the test stand and putting the pump into service.
• E-Tech manager will provide a procedure for the established gas train and the testing procedure in an SOP for running gas including all hookup and parts that are approved.

narrative: A worker fell approximately 16 feet from an aerial work platform onto a Christmas tree cart. The incident occurred while the worker was using a rope tied to the basket to pull an umbilical and create slack for a storm loop. The rope failed under tension, releasing stored energy that transferred to the basket. This sudden release caused the basket to jolt, ejecting the worker.
what_went_wrong: The task was executed outside equipment design intent, with a man-riding work basket simultaneously used to pull a load, creating uncontrolled stored energy and disabling effective engineered safeguards. The activity was not recognised or managed as a lifting operation, resulting in inadequate planning, inappropriate equipment selection, and exposure of a person to the line of fire when the rope failed. These failures were reinforced by unclear procedures, fragmented task briefings, and ineffective supervision, allowing unsafe deviations to become normalised.
corrective_actions:
1. Inspection and maintenance for man-riding and lifting equipment must meet or exceed manufacturer requirements, particularly under heavy or harsh operating conditions. Inspection scope, frequency, and competency should scale with equipment usage and environmental exposure - not minimum internal checklists.
2. Checklist effectiveness depends as much on quality, compliance, and competency as the checklist itself. Poor design, superficial completion, or unclear roles can create false assurance and allow serious hazards to persist.
3. Safe operation of critical equipment requires clear, shared accountability across suppliers, contractors, and asset owners. Pre-mobilization checks, acceptance inspections, condition monitoring, and post-event inspections must be treated as mandatory control points throughout the equipment lifecycle - not administrative steps.

narrative: Following heavy rainfall, landslide occurred in the area behind the ten wagon-type cabins (accommodation, canteen, washing, changing, and rest facilities) located at the oil well site. A ground instability and multiple surface cracks were identified in the surrounding area. Personnel were immediately informed of the hazardous ground conditions and instructed to remain vigilant and exercise caution. As a preventive control measure, the wagon-type units were relocated to a safer area to eliminate the risk of impact from further ground movement.
what_went_wrong:
• Inadequate assessment of ground stability.
• Insufficient drainage and erosion control measures.
• Lack of preventive geotechnical monitoring.
• Temporary facilities positioned in potentially hazardous zone.
corrective_actions:
• A geotechnical assessment should be conducted before positioning cabins, especially in areas prone to heavy rainfall, slopes, or loose soil conditions.
• Effective surface water drainage and erosion control measures must be implemented to prevent water accumulation and soil weakening.
• Surface cracks and minor soil movement must be treated as serious warning indicators. A formal inspection and reporting system should be established for ground condition monitoring.
• Heavy rainfall scenarios should be included in site risk assessments, particularly for temporary infrastructure.

what_went_wrong:

• Insufficient communication with vessel captain.

corrective_actions:
• Ensure all vessels operating near offshore platforms are aware of ongoing diving operations.
• Strengthen coordination with support vessels and vessel traffic control to enforce exclusion zones proactively.
• Establish mandatory pre-approach notifications for all vessels near the platform.
• Ensure immediate and continuous communication channels between the platform, diving team, and vessel captains.

For causes yet to be determined, an actuated valve (SDV) located near the installation area -resting vertically on the ground and not involved in the lifting operation - lost its vertical stability and fell, resulting in a person being crushed between the valve and the skid structure.
what_went_wrong: The injured person released the rigging that was securing the SDV valve. After the rigging was removed, the injured person remained in the line of fire.
corrective_actions: Comply with the Planning Cycle, with a focus on scheduling work based on available resources (time, personnel, competencies, and equipment). Consistently ensure competencies (knowledge, skills, and psycho-physical fitness) aligned with each role within the Work Control System and the Technical Practices, Procedures, and Regulations associated with the activity. Promote the execution of activities with a strong sense of vulnerability, full awareness, and sound judgment, and empower personnel to feel authorized to stop any activity they consider unsafe, as the last barrier to prevent Undesired Events.

narrative: Crew shuttle collision during a braking manoeuvre, the shuttle initially collided with the vehicle in front, then crossed into the oncoming lane and was struck on the right side by a semi-trailer truck traveling in the opposite direction.
what_went_wrong:
1. The driver did not slow down to maintain a safe following distance.
2. The contractor company has not defined a designated rest area or conditions for the drivers; they rest in the vehicles.
3. The unit's Active Brake Assist system was not operational.
corrective_actions:
1. Incorporate into the mobility plan the tables of maximum permitted speeds and rest rules.
2. Install a sleeping trailer to ensure adequate rest conditions for contractor drivers on site.
3. Define the necessary active safety standards in personnel transport units, including new technologies (ADAS).

narrative: During maintenance work at a Generation Unit, the mechanical technician suffered a fall from height, falling to a lower level from the engine access platform.
what_went_wrong: During corrective maintenance work on turbochargers and the replacement of cylinder head at Generation Unit, the mechanic suffered a fall to a lower level (3.30 m), falling from the engine access platform to the shelter floor.
corrective_actions: Ensure that procedures or work instructions clearly include the step-by-step sequence of the activity to be performed. The Job Safety Analysis (JSA) must identify all hazards inherent to the activity. Let us reinforce risk analysis for critical activities (falls to a lower level). Combat the normalization of deviations. Do not take shortcuts when performing tasks; always comply with established procedures. Take control and apply the Stop Work Policy whenever you identify an unsafe condition: stop, correct, and then continue.

narrative: During the heating of an 18-inch pipe to remove the coating, the worker placed the torch at the entrance of the 18-inch pipe. When attempting to light the torch with a manual spark igniter, a flammable atmosphere was created, causing a flash fire that resulted in first and second-degree burns to the worker's face after being hit sideways by a flash fire in the manufacturing workshop area.
what_went_wrong:
• The torch was not in optimal condition (the built-in/manual spark igniter did not work properly).
• Low perception of risk when lighting a torch in a closed environment.
• Incorrect Work Permit (PTW), classified the activity as "cold work" when in fact it involved "high-energy hot work" with the generation of ignition sources.
corrective_actions:
• Emphasize the responsibilities of workers with roles in the PTW system in the event of serious or fatal workplace accidents involving their own workers or contractors.
• Conduct an awareness campaign (including contractors) on inspection, reporting, and replacement of tools and equipment in poor condition (homemade or artisanal tools) before the end of the year.

narrative:
During production tubing running operations on the drilling rig, four metallic components fell from height while using the catline system.
• Objects dropped from approximately 40 m height
• 2 × 1.8 kg (≈ 706 J each)
• 2 × 10.4 kg (≈ 4,076 J each) The falling energy was sufficient to cause a fatality. No injuries occurred, but this qualifies as a High Potential Event (HIPO) due to the severe dropped-object energy.
what_went_wrong:
• Catline anchoring point and installation were modified from the original design without engineering review.
• Assembly was improperly installed and inadequately supported (misaligned rods/spacers, gaps in fittings).
• Refurbished and reused components were not integrity tested; the installed system was not certified to required load capacity.
• No Management of Change (MOC), risk assessment, or formal operator approval for the modification.
• PTW/JSA did not address the installation change or dropped-object risk.
• Poor communication and oversight between operator and contractor; no operator supervision of the work.
corrective_actions:
• Treat any change to lifting/hoisting equipment or anchoring as a design change requiring MOC, risk assessment, and operator approval.
• Certification must cover the complete installed system, not only individual components, and must meet operational load requirements.
• Verify integrity of reused or refurbished parts before use.
• Ensure PTW/JSA reflects actual installation and hazards.
• Clearly define contractor-operator responsibilities and provide supervision for safety-critical work.
• Conduct formal dropped-object inspections after maintenance or modification to derrick equipment.

narrative: On 22 March at approximately 08:45, a tool bag was lifted from the rig floor to the derrick using catline #02 during equipment mobilisation. When the bag reached the derrickman's platform level, it suddenly accelerated upward, struck the sheave, the bag handles failed, and the bag and tools fell, impacting a container on the deck below. No injuries occurred, but the dropped object had fatality potential.
what_went_wrong:
• Catline was used improperly for lifting a tool bag.
• Personnel lacked adequate training/competence in catline operation.
• Work scope changed without risk assessment.
• JSA/permit requirements were not properly followed (not signed by all participants).
• Poor communication and coordination between personnel during the lift.
corrective_actions:
• Only trained and authorised personnel should operate catline/hoisting equipment.
• Conduct a risk assessment and update the JSA whenever the work scope changes.
• Verify communication and clear roles between workers before lifting activities.
• Ensure lifting of tools uses appropriate lifting containers and certified lifting methods.
• Reinforce compliance with PTW/JSA participation and pre-job briefings.

narrative: On 17 November at approximately 09:40, the smoke detector in the laundry room activated after several cleaning cloths spontaneously combusted shortly after being removed from a dryer and placed on the floor. The fire brigade responded immediately and extinguished the fire using CO2 and dry powder extinguishers. No injuries or asset damage occurred, but the event had potential for a serious fire and smoke exposure.
what_went_wrong:
• Cleaning cloths were likely contaminated with a chemical/oily substance capable of self-heating after drying.
• The chemical hazard was not identified prior to washing and drying.
• Hot cloths were stacked/placed on the floor immediately after drying, allowing heat build-up and ignition.
• No procedure or segregation process existed for handling contaminated rags.
• Personnel did not recognise the chemical odour as a hazard indicator.
corrective_actions:
• Treat cleaning rags as potentially oil/chemical contaminated materials.
• Implement segregation and identification of contaminated cloths before laundering.
• Allow hot cloths to cool in a ventilated metal container or spread individually -do not pile them.
• Provide training on spontaneous combustion risks (especially oils, solvents, and hydrocarbons).
• Establish procedures for laundering and disposal of contaminated rags.
• Provide dedicated fire-safe storage bins for used cleaning cloths.

narrative: On 27 December at approximately 07:30, cleaning cloths contaminated with cooking oil were washed and dried in the laundry. After drying, the cloths were placed on the floor inside an open bag next to other cloths. Later, all laundry ventilation, exhaust, and air-conditioning systems were switched off while the room was unattended. At approximately 13:15, the cloths began releasing smoke and an incipient fire developed. The steward used a dry chemical extinguisher and the fire brigade extinguished the fire. No injuries or damage occurred, but the event had serious fire potential.
what_went_wrong:
• Oil-contaminated cloths were washed and dried without special handling precautions.
• Hot cloths were stored in a pile/bag, allowing heat accumulation and self-heating.
• Laundry ventilation and cooling were shut down while the cloths were unattended.
• No procedure existed for segregation, cooling, or disposal of oily rags.
• Hazard of spontaneous combustion from oil-soaked rags was not recognised.
corrective_actions:
• Segregate oil/grease contaminated cloths before laundering.
• Do not place recently dried cloths in piles, bags, or enclosed areas - allow them to cool individually in a ventilated metal container or spread out.
• Maintain ventilation/exhaust until materials have cooled.
• Implement procedures for handling and disposal of contaminated rags.
• Train personnel on spontaneous combustion risks (oils, hydrocarbons, solvents).
• Provide fire-resistant rag bins and designated storage areas.

narrative: During a pull-out operation on the platform, an uncommanded movement of the vessel's aft reel occurred, exposing a worker to a potentially fatal risk.
what_went_wrong: Failure in reel control/safeguarding (locking/brake/holding system), as the equipment was not properly secured, resulting in uncommanded movement.
corrective_actions: Always ensure reels and rotating equipment are properly secured using effective locking, braking, or holding systems to prevent uncommanded movement and associated hazards.
